entries.title: Man fatally stabbed during fight in Calumet Heights
entries.summary: <p>A man is dead after being stabbed during a fight in Calumet Heights Wednesday evening, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The man, whose age wasn’t known, was involved in an altercation with someone near the 1400 block of East 87th Street at 6:54 p.m. when he was stabbed multiple times, police said. The wounded man was taken to University of Chicago Medical Center where he later died.</p><p>No one is in custody, police said. An investigation is ongoing.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: White Sox burn both ABS challenges in third inning of Game 3 ALDS loss to Guardians
entries.summary: <p>The White Sox have maintained all year that empowering their players to be aggressive with ABS challenges of umpires’ ball-and-strike calls will pay larger dividends on balance, even if it entails some nights where the club burns through both their ABS challenges in short order.</p><p>They probably hoped such a scenario didn't take place in the third inning of Game 3 of the American League Division Series, as catcher <b>Kyle Teel</b>–who had been 7-for-8 in the postseason entering Wednesday–lost both ABS challenges in successive plate appearances while trying to guide a wild <b>Bryan Hudson</b> through a disastrous, four-run frame.</p><p>“I felt good, he put a good swing on it,” said <b>Hagen Smith</b>, who relieved Hudson but yielded a bases-clearing triple to <b>Jo Adell </b>that put two more runs on Hudson’s tab.</p><p>Did the lack of challenges contribute to an ugly afternoon where the White Sox lost the battle of the strike zone, with their pitchers issuing 10 walks and their hitters punching out 19 times? It didn’t help, but it would be hard for the ABS system to carry that much weight.</p><p>“Just need to be better,” said Teel. “Bad game for me [with] challenging. Learn from it, do better tomorrow, but it’s got to be better.”</p><p>The Sox further lost a replay challenge in the bottom of the fourth, immediately after the Guardians successfully challenged that left-hander <b>Foster Griffin</b>’s pitch did not hit <b>Tristan Peters</b> in the hand but instead hit his bat. Sox manager <b>Will Venable </b>countered by challenging that<b> </b>catcher <b>Patrick Bailey </b>had committed catcher’s interference on Peters’ check-swing, but to no avail.</p><p>This all took place in the second pitch of the at-bat, before Peters eventually doubled home <b>Chase Meidroth </b>on the ninth.</p><p><b>Antonacci did his part</b></p><p>White Sox rookie <b>Sam Antonacci</b> usually defines his job on offense as just getting on base, especially when facing fellow left-handers. It’s hard to quibble with his work in a losing effort on Wednesday.</p><p>Antonacci’s only hit came on a medium-speed ground ball up the middle off lefty <b>Joey Cantillo</b>. Yet he reached base four times, including scoring after a leadoff walk in the first. The other two times? You’re supposed to lean on your strengths in the postseason, and MLB’s hit-by-pitch leader was plunked twice in Game 3, including to force home a run with the bases loaded in the sixth.</p><p><b>Playoff atmosphere</b></p><p>A mistake-filled blowout loss did not put White Sox players in an especially reflective mood about fan support, but there are only so many chances to play in front of 40,590 screaming fans dressed in all black.</p><p>“To be real honest, I was a little emotional,” said right-hander <b>Davis Martin</b>, the team’s longest-tenured player. “National anthem, like just seeing it all and experiencing what we went through in [2024], and just to get back to this point was unbelievable.”</p><p>The Sox will be leaning on fan support again on Thursday, with another chance to clinch a bid to the American League Championship Series.</p><p>“They’ve been amazing all year,” said Meidroth. “We wouldn’t have been in this spot without them and we’re looking forward to [Thursday].”</p><p><b>Scoreboard watching</b></p><p>With the Yankees down 2-0 and facing elimination in their ALDS matchup against the Rays, whether they can stay alive affects the White Sox’ Game 4 start time. Sox-Guardians is scheduled for 4pm CT, but will shift to 7pm if the Yankees lose.</p>
entries.author: James Fegan

entries.title: Will White Sox ever win a postseason series in Chicago? After losing Game 3, they're down to their last shot
entries.summary: <p>They’re dying to dance in the streets of Bridgeport and Armour Square, Back of the Yards and Beverly, Roseland and Hegewisch, Calumet Park and South Holland.</p><p>Oh, so ready to raise a glass at Bernice’s Tavern and Shinnick’s Pub, at Cork & Kerry and Jimmy’s Woodlawn Tap.</p><p>And to break bread with gleeful goodwill at Fat Johnnie’s, Vito & Nick’s, Valois, Daley’s and the Duck Inn.</p><p>For once, the South Side wants to see its beloved <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> clinch a postseason series in Chicago, something that hasn’t occurred since — if you can believe it — the 1906 World Series against the Cubs.</p><p>Those Cubs had a winning percentage of .763, still the highest in baseball’s modern era. Those Sox were so bad at swinging the sticks, they were known as the “Hitless Wonders.” The Sox won anyway, which, of course, not a damn one of us remembers.</p><p>But now there’s a division series against the Guardians, and a Sox team that arrived at Rate Field on Wednesday leading two games to none in a best-of-five.</p><p>A “Blackout” in the stands. Towels waving. Fans aroar. And — what a letdown — a 9-3 Sox defeat.</p><p>That leaves <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/10/07/chicago-white-sox-cleveland-guardians-will-venable-miguel-vargas-kyle-teel-chase-meidroth-mlb-playoffs-postseason" target="_blank" >one more shot Thursday for the Sox to clinch at home</a>. By God, it’s time for it to finally happen. The 1917 Sox won the World Series over the New York Giants at the Polo Grounds. The 2005 champs enjoyed clinchers in Boston, Anaheim and Houston. This year’s team swept the Astros in the wild-card round in Houston. The South Side needs a celebration.</p><p>Either that or win Game 5 back in Cleveland, but who wants to bet on that?</p><p>The odds remain in the Sox’ favor, for what it’s worth. Right around 90% of major league teams that have led 2-0 in best-of-five series have ended up happy.</p><p>But the Guardians are busting with confidence after getting off the schneid.</p><p>“I would say our confidence is at a 10 [out of 10],” said pitcher Gavin Williams, the American League’s strikeout champion, who would get the ball in Game 5 if he doesn’t appear in relief in Game 4 and the Guardians remain alive. “It better be a 10.”</p><p>The Sox will have to tangle again with the Guardians’ top starter this season, Parker Messick, in Game 4.</p><p>“I’m ready to rock and roll,” Messick said.</p><p>But the Sox are ready to frame and hang more newspaper pages in the Rate press box. Yes, newspapers still exist — don’t even joke about that — and dated ones mark all the biggest Sox occasions on the walls where the home and visiting scribes sit.</p><p>The Sun-Times cover pages alone are wonderful to see. “EL, YES!” in big, fat headline type after Orlando “El Duque” Hernandez pitched the Sox past the Red Sox in 2005. “WORLD CLASS” after the Sox got past the Angels that year. “CHAMPS!” after they won it all against the Astros. “SOXAPALOOZA!” after the downtown parade.</p><p>The press box is screaming for an image of the Sox piling onto the mound right here at home.</p><p>Jose Abreu didn’t win a postseason series here. Mark Buerhle, Frank Thomas, Harold Baines, Dick Allen, Luis Aparicio, Minnie Minoso, Nellie Fox — none of them. You get the picture.</p><p>What better time than now, when there are no paper bags over heads and no “Sell the team!” signs in the crowd?</p><p>The Sox are only the fourth team ever to appear in the postseason a year after losing 100 games, and they’re the one and only team to do so after losing 100 games back-to-back (or, in the Sox’ case, back-to-back-to-back). It’s still crazy that they’re even in this position, but they might as well not foul it up now, right?</p><p>Again, though, the Guardians, accustomed to being better than their division rivals, have their chests puffed out.</p><p>“We’ve got to stand on something,” said outfielder Steven Kwan, who drove in his team’s first run on a win-or-go-home late afternoon.</p><div class="Enhancement" Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Jose Ramirez, the Guardians’ best player, has been a Sox nemesis for longer than a decade and was the star of this game with his bat, his legs and his glove. When he doubled to left, stole third and came flying home on an infield grounder in the fifth, beating second baseman Chase Meidroth’s throw, all the game’s momentum went with him.</p><p>“That made it a Jose Ramirez game,” Kwan said.</p><p>In the sixth, Ramirez made a diving stop of a Miguel Vargas smash with the bases loaded and two out and the Sox down just 5-3.</p><p>“After that I felt like, ‘This is going to be our game,’ ” Ramirez said via a translator.</p><p>It was game on. Now it’s series on.</p><p>“We came here to compete,” Ramirez said. “That’s what [the Sox] did when they weren’t at home. They won two games. We can do it, too.”</p><p>There’s a question Guardians manager Stephen Vogt often asks his team: “What do you like better, making 50,000 people go crazy or shutting 50,000 people up?”</p><p>One happens at home and the other on the road, of course.</p><p>“Both very different feelings,” Vogt said, “but they’re equally as fun.”</p><p>But nothing tops winning a postseason series on your home turf. The Sox and their fans wouldn’t know this, but they can ask around.</p><p>There’s one more shot at it. The headline awaits.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/10/07/chicago-white-sox-cleveland-guardians-will-venable-miguel-vargas-kyle-teel-chase-meidroth-mlb-playoffs-postseason" target="_blank" >White Sox believe in tomorrow — but there are only so many left</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: White Sox put on worst performance in weeks, in front of first home playoff crowd in years
entries.summary: <p>Will Venable’s ballclub proved him right on Wednesday in Game 3 of the American League Division Series, albeit not in a way he appreciated.</p><p>“Talked about this the whole series, that these guys are going to make you pay for walks,” Venable said postgame. “First couple games, they didn't. But today, they did.”</p><p>After defying that axiom in a rocky first inning of their Game 2 win in Cleveland, the Sox and 40,590 supporters were dragged back to reality in a 9-3 blowout loss in Game 3. Sox pitching issued 10 free passes (one intentional) to Guardians hitters, while their hitters struck out 19 times; an MLB postseason record for a nine-inning game</p><p>“They just controlled the zone well,” said catcher Kyle Teel.</p><p>The Sox walked eight Guardians hitters in two games in Cleveland, and actually only three in Game 2. But Bryan Hudson and Hagen Smith combined for three in a four-run third alone, capped off by a bases-clearing Jo Adell triple that put the Guardians up for good.</p><p>“Just the pitching staff as a whole, minimizing walks and leadoff walks,” said Davis Martin–who issued two himself in the ninth–when asked what was missing from the Sox effort. “That [the Guardians’] lineup in general. They work hard [at-bats], they know the zone.”</p><p>Venable’s pre-series warning applied to not just walks, but allowing stolen bases and defensive misplays. All free bases yielded to the opponent needed to be trimmed from their diet.</p><p>Instead, the first of two Guardians stolen bases led to a run, with Jose Ramirez nabbing third after a one-out double in the fifth, allowing him to score on a hard grounder to Chase Meidroth. Playing from behind and not in position to deploy their best outfield defenders, Ramirez’s two-run bloop triple dropped beyond Randal Grichuk’s dive to put things out of reach in the eighth, before Miguel Vargas lost track of Brayan Rocchio’s pop behind third base to plate another run in the ninth.</p><p>“A lot of times during the year we lost tough games, and we bounced back the next day,” said Vargas. “That’s what we do.”</p><p>The Sox had no losing streaks longer than four, no winning streaks longer than five this year. With four playoff wins after winning their regular season finale, maybe they hit their cap and were due for their worst performance in weeks, unfortunately during the first home playoff crowd at Rate Field in five years.</p><p>“This is what we’ve been doing all year,” said Sean Newcomb, the only Sox pitcher who didn’t issue a walk over his two scoreless innings as opener.</p><p>But the longer this series stretches on, the trickier it becomes for the White Sox to navigate the Guardians’ starting pitching advantage. It was on display even with both sides running bullpen games on Wednesday, as All-Star left-hander Foster Griffin worked in bulk and recorded a Guardians’ record seven strikeouts as a reliever, and the Sox bullpen saw their control abandon them amid weeks of heavy use.</p><p>Of the five Sox pitchers on the ALDS roster who didn’t pitch Wednesday, two are high-leverage relievers (Grant Taylor and Jordan Hicks), two are starters who have only appeared in relief so far (Anthony Kay and Erick Fedde) and one is pretty essential to any Game 5 plans (Sean Burke). True to form, the Sox have not announced a Game 4 starter as of press time, and will likely be piecing things together as they go, figuring out which arms are available during pre-game catch play.</p><p>For their part, the Guardians are starting likely AL Cy Young finalist Parker Messick on regular rest.</p><p>“We’ve seen him a lot, I think that helps and our gameplan against him will be similar,” said outfielder Tristan Peters. “We've been resilient the whole season. Why can't we do it now?”</p><p>No insurmountable reason comes to mind. But if they don’t, it’ll be hard to remember all the times they did.</p>
entries.author: James Fegan

entries.title: White Sox believe in tomorrow — but there are only so many left
entries.summary: <p>Everyone has a plan until they get punched in the mouth.</p><p>Heavyweight champ Mike Tyson spoke those words about 30 years ago, and they often proved prophetic after his opponent entered the ring. The man had 44 knockouts. That’s a lot of plans getting torn up.</p><p>For the first time this postseason, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> took a punch in the mouth. They suffered their first loss Wednesday, falling to the Guardians 9-3. After beating the Astros twice in the wild-card series and taking the first two in the division series, the Sox find themselves in a new position — having to bounce back from a playoff defeat.</p><p>When the Sox were knocked down in the regular season, they didn’t stay down long. Their longest losing streak was four games, and it took them until August to reach it. That was impressive, but they don’t have that kind of time here. The ref is starting his 10-count.</p><p>“We’ve done it all year,” manager Will Venable said. “We’ve been in tough spots where we haven’t played our best games, we’ve played good games. Whatever the result, these guys came back the next day. It’s really been the story of our group, being able to bounce back no matter what happens.”</p><p>What happened Wednesday was the Sox struck out 19 times. In case you forgot, a team gets 27 outs in baseball. That means the Sox didn’t put the ball in play nearly as much as they needed to. They had six hits.</p><p>The Sox can’t chase pitches Thursday in Game 4 against left-handed starter Parker Messick, who had 193 strikeouts in the regular season, tied for 15th in baseball. If they do, it won’t get any easier in Game 5. The Guardians have righty Gavin Williams, the American League strikeout leader with 248, lined up. Can the Sox beat either again?</p><p>But let’s focus on one crisis at a time. In fact, let’s take a deep breath and take a cue from the Sox, who are convinced they’ve been here before — even though they really haven’t.</p><p>“A lot of times during the year, we lost tough games, and we bounced back the next day,” third baseman Miguel Vargas said. “That’s what we do. We have a short memory, I guess. We’re going to be ready for tomorrow.”</p><p>“Today has nothing to do with tomorrow. Nothing,” catcher Kyle Teel said defiantly. “We come ready to go like we always do tomorrow.”</p><p>The Sox do have some things going for them. They didn’t need Grant Taylor and his mechanical right arm in Game 3. That means he’ll have a whole extra day of rest before Game 4 than he did before Game 2, when he earned the save just two days after pitching four innings to close out Game 1.</p><p>However, Taylor was shaky on the seven pitches he threw Monday. He gave Sox fans a palpitation on his first pitch, nearly allowing a game-tying home run to Jo Adell. His next pitch was a drive to deep left that was caught. Nursing a one-run lead in the ninth, he allowed back-to-back, scary-deep flies to center.</p><p>In 5 ⅓ innings this series, Taylor has allowed three hits and struck out six with no walks. But that outing could portend trouble.</p><p>Hagen Smith, the Sox’ other reliable reliever — or opener or whatever you want to call him — wasn’t so reliable Wednesday. Entering a 1-1 game in the third, he walked the first batter he faced, Jose Ramirez, to load the bases and was one strike away from getting out of trouble when Jo Adell tripled.</p><p>Smith hadn’t allowed a run in 5 ⅔ innings in the postseason, but he walked three in Game 1 against the Guardians. He said he could pitch Thursday, but he might need a break.</p><p>The Sox could have more trouble if Munetaka Murakami can’t rediscover his stroke from Cleveland, where he went 3-for-8 with a home run and three RBI. On Wednesday, the Guardians game-planned for him perfectly, having him face four pitchers, the last three of them lefties. He went 0-for-4 with three strikeouts.</p><p>That said, his home run in Game 1 came against Messick, whom the Sox knocked out in the fifth inning. See? It’s not all bad.</p><p>“It’s baseball. You’re not going to win every game,” second baseman Chase Meidroth said. “That’s the reality of it. But tomorrow is a new day; it’s a new game.”</p><p>That it is, but in a five-game series, there are only so many days left.</p>

entries.title: Caleb Wilson makes Bulls debut and does so with no shortage of bravado
entries.summary: <p>It wasn’t a highlight.</p><p>It wasn’t even that memorable.</p><p>With 6:01 left in the first quarter of Wednesday’s preseason opener with the Suns, Caleb Wilson pivoted, spun, and hit a 20-foot mid-range shot for his first NBA basket.</p><p>A nice moment for the Bulls’ No. 4 overall pick, but Wilson wasn’t looking for nice. This is a movement as far as Wilson was concerned. An organizational shift in which he’s one of the foundation pieces that’s been assigned to turn the fortunes of the franchise around.</p><p>Not with nice moments, either. With highlights. With jaw-dropping, high-flying highlights that serve notice of his arrival. Yes, done within the framework of playing winning basketball – evident by the 124-117 win over Phoenix – but also not shying away from chasing down individual goals like NBA Rookie of the Year honors.</p><p>He reiterated that once again.</p><p>“Preseason might not count statistically or anything like that, but honestly we’re all visual and if you see something that you think is impressive, you’re going to gravitate towards it,” Wilson said. “My first impression for the league and myself and my team (started Wednesday).”</p><p>He did finally have some “visual” moments in the second quarter, first with a breakaway dunk and then with a smooth reverse layup that drew the foul. With a loaded rookie class, however – especially at the top – the campaign will need more umph to it than 15 points on 6-of-15 shooting (0-of-4 from three-point range).</p><p>Wilson was confident that there would be plenty more to come.</p><p>What he wanted to show against Phoenix, besides a few SportsCenter Top 10s, was his defensive side of the ball. An area he had been working on.</p><p>“I always felt like I could guard but the NBA is way more physical, a lot more communication, so I’ve been working on that,” Wilson said.</p><p>Call that a work in progress after Game 1 because there were some issues there.</p><p>That could be said about a lot of the Bulls players in the preseason debut.</p><p>The Bulls jumped out to a quick 18-13 lead with the starters, as Matas Buzelis, Norman Powell and Jalen Smith each came out hunting shots.</p><p>The problem was when coach Tiago Splitter had to go to the bench, once again pressing rookie Dailyn Swain into ball-handling duties with Tre Jones out with a sore hip. Swain didn’t get a lot of help but also didn’t help himself, struggling with ball-handling like he did back in Summer League.</p><p>Swain played just 3:23 of the first quarter and was a minus-10 in plus/minus with a turnover. He played another four-plus minutes in the second and had another turnover with three fouls.</p><p>The starters did come to the rescue after that. Powell put up 14 points in his 14 minutes of work and didn’t play in the second half, while Buzelis scored 10 of his 14 points in the first half.</p><p>As far as Wilson making that early impression, Splitter obviously had a different way of looking at it.</p><p>“He really is saying everything that goes through his mind,” the coach said of Wilson. “He’s being honest. He wants to be a great player, he wants to win Rookie of the Year, a lot of the things, but he also works for it.</p><p>“I don’t love those individual awards, let’s say. I think if you do the right thing he’s going to get there. Yes, he’s speaking all of those things but he still has a lot to do.”</p><p>That’s why Wilson gave himself what he thought was a fair grade for his first game.</p><p>“Probably a B,” Wilson said. “I made mistakes but that’s to be expected. Also knowing that most of the stuff I messed up on I can fix.”</p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Mother's chats with grown daughter are criticized by fiance
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My fiance gets annoyed and calls it weird that I talk to my daughter every morning on my way to work and in the afternoon on my way home. She's a wife and young mother of two, ages 1 and 4. I'm proud of how well she is doing.</p><p>I work full time, and she works part time. We're both always busy, so we don't see each other as often as we'd like, even though we live in the same town. At 25, my daughter is becoming my best friend. I love helping her through decisions, ideas, etc. I don't agree with my fiance that this is "weird." I believe mothers and daughters who are close do this.</p><p>What's your opinion about this? How can I better explain to my fiance that this isn't taking anything away from him? — <i>MOTHERING IN MASSACHUSETTS</i></p><p><b>DEAR MOTHERING:</b> You are extremely fortunate to have such a warm relationship with your daughter. You can explain this until you're blue in the face, but if your fiance feels that he, and not your daughter, should be your best friend, it will be like talking to a wall.</p><p>From where I sit, for your fiance to dictate how often you talk with your daughter — when you're not with him — is more than a little bit controlling. It's time to ask yourself if his need to control manifests itself in other ways. If it does, you may want to reconsider his status as fiance.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> One of my neighbors keeps their dog tied outside for long periods of time. I often see him shivering and pacing, and he barks and cries late into the night. I don't know my neighbor well, and I don't want to cause conflict or make assumptions. At the same time, it's hard to ignore what I'm seeing and hearing, especially when the temperatures drop below freezing. I've thought about saying something or even reporting it, but I worry about overstepping or making the situation worse. What's the right thing to do? — <i>CONCERNED IN THE COLD</i></p><p><b>DEAR CONCERNED:</b> You can't possibly make the situation worse, so why not try to make it better? Research the appropriate authority for your area (usually Animal Control) and report what you've seen and heard. It's up to them to determine whether your neighbor's actions constitute abuse and what to do from there. If you do, you'll feel better and you may save the poor animal from a lifetime of suffering.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> A dear friend of mine, "Connie," told me of a situation she has with her husband. This man will not let her use his cellphone in an emergency. He said his phone is for his private use only. When Connie and her husband moved to a different state, he stayed behind and followed the family several days later. Do you think Connie should have concerns about her marriage? — <i>CURIOUS IN PENNSYLVANIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR CURIOUS:</b> What you and I think matters far less than what Connie thinks. Between you and me, I find that people who act in a secretive way usually have something to hide. However, you should not stir the pot. If you want to be helpful, stay out of it.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: Making executions less ugly to watch doesn't make them quicker or reliable
entries.summary: <p>After Tennessee unsuccessfully <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/us/christa-pike-stay-execution-tennessee.html" target="_blank" >tried</a> to execute Christa Pike last week, an ambulance whisked her to a Nashville hospital, where the condemned <a class="Link" href="https://archive.knoxnews.com/news/local/pike-guilty-of-murder-ep-894326802-353645051.html/" target="_blank" >murderer</a> became a <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/01/us/tennessee-executions-christa-pike-lee-review.html" target="_blank" >patient</a> in urgent need of lifesaving care. Should Pike recover from two botched administrations of pentobarbital, which left her unconscious and unable to breathe on her own, she might travel that road in reverse after she is well enough to be killed.</p><p>That bizarre episode illustrates the perverse consequences of trying to <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2008/04/23/think-of-it-as-a-lifectomy/" target="_blank" >disguise</a> the brutal reality of capital punishment by <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2014/07/29/a-lethal-injection-of-reality/" target="_blank" >dressing it</a> in medical garb. Although most Americans say murderers like Pike should be executed, the method they prefer suggests they are squeamish about admitting what that entails.</p><p>Last year, Gallup put <a class="Link" href="https://news.gallup.com/poll/1606/death-penalty.aspx" target="_blank" >support</a> for the death penalty at 52%, 28 percentage points lower than the peak recorded in 1994. According to several surveys, Americans overwhelmingly <a class="Link" href="https://news.gallup.com/poll/1606/death-penalty.aspx" target="_blank" >view</a> lethal injection, first adopted by Oklahoma in 1977, as "the most humane" method of execution, preferring it to firing squads, hanging, the electric chair and the gas chamber.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-8a0000" name="module-8a0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>The Supreme Court embraced that view in 2008, when it <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2008/04/23/think-of-it-as-a-lifectomy/" target="_blank" >upheld</a> Kentucky's three-drug execution method, which critics portrayed as iffy and needlessly complicated. At that point, three dozen states had adopted lethal injection, which Chief Justice John Roberts <a class="Link" href="https://tile.loc.gov/storage-services/service/ll/usrep/usrep553/usrep553035/usrep553035.pdf" target="_blank" >described</a> as the result of "an earnest desire to provide for a progressively more humane manner of death."</p><p>As Roberts saw it, lethal injection was "more humane" than "the firing squad, hanging, the electric chair and the gas chamber." But while lethal injection might look less ugly than those older methods, appearances can be deceptive.</p><p>As Fordham University law professor Deborah Denno noted a few months before that decision, execution methods that are less painful to watch may not be less painful to experience.</p><p>"To me," she <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2008/01/03/world/americas/03iht-03lethal.9002408.html" target="_blank" >told</a> The New York Times, "the firing squad is the most humane," although it is "perceived to be the most brutal."</p><p>Since then, most death penalty states have shifted to a single-drug protocol, typically involving a lethal dose of pentobarbital. But as the attempted execution of Pike shows, that change has not eliminated the <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/04/opinion/christa-pike-botched-execution.html" target="_blank" >challenge</a> of finding a usable vein and making sure the drug enters the bloodstream rather than surrounding tissue — a task that can be complicated by preexisting medical conditions.</p><p>Pike's aborted lethal injection was the <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/21/us/tennessee-execution.html" target="_blank" >second</a> such failure in Tennessee this year, and it prompted Gov. Bill Lee to <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/01/us/tennessee-executions-christa-pike-lee-review.html" target="_blank" >suspend</a> executions until he can clarify exactly what went wrong. But last week's "tragedy" (as Lee described it) was just the latest example of a <a class="Link" href="https://deathpenaltyinfo.org/executions/botched-executions" target="_blank" >problem</a> that goes back more than 40 years: <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2014/07/29/a-lethal-injection-of-reality/" target="_blank" >prolonged lethal injections</a> featuring disturbing signs of the needless suffering that the method is supposed to avoid.</p><p>Lethal injection drugs, which are difficult to source because pharmaceutical companies are loath to supply them, also have proven to be <a class="Link" href="https://utahnewsdispatch.com/2024/08/20/cost-of-utah-execution-taberon-honie/" target="_blank" >exorbitantly expensive</a>, costing <a class="Link" href="https://deathpenaltyinfo.org/governor-says-indiana-will-not-purchase-more-lethal-injection-drugs-invites-debate-over-death-penalty" target="_blank" >as much as $300,000</a> for each dose of pentobarbital. And since the drug degrades relatively quickly, much of that money may be wasted when pentobarbital goes unused for longer than its 90-day shelf life.</p><p>Largely for those reasons, legislators are <a class="Link" href="https://deathpenaltyinfo.org/governor-says-indiana-will-not-purchase-more-lethal-injection-drugs-invites-debate-over-death-penalty" target="_blank" >reconsidering</a> the virtues of firing squads, which five states currently <a class="Link" href="https://deathpenaltyinfo.org/research/analysis/reports/year-end-reports/the-death-penalty-in-2025/legislation" target="_blank" >allow</a> in at least some circumstances. Condemned killers also see an advantage: Last year in South Carolina, three prisoners <a class="Link" href="https://deathpenaltyinfo.org/executions/methods-of-execution/description-of-each-method" target="_blank" >chose</a> the firing squad over lethal injection.</p><p>It is not hard to see why. Reviewing cases from 1890 through 2010, the Death Penalty Information Center <a class="Link" href="https://deathpenaltyinfo.org/executions/botched-executions" target="_blank" >found</a> that lethal injection had the highest rate of botched executions: about 7%, compared to 5% for lethal gas, 3% for hanging and 2% for electrocution. The rate for firing squads was 0%.</p><p>Such evidence underlines a point that states overlooked in their rush to embrace lethal injection: Prettifying executions does not necessarily make them quicker or more reliable. The <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/10/02/would-a-firing-squad-have-been-more-humane-for-christa-pike/" target="_blank" >quest</a> for "more humane" execution methods, ostensibly an effort to minimize the discomfort of condemned criminals, actually aims to relieve the public's discomfort with killing people in cold blood.</p><p><i>Jacob Sullum is a senior editor at Reason magazine.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-8f0000" name="module-8f0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Ex-Gangster Disciples enforcer goes to trial for $345K share of wrongfully convicted man's settlement
entries.summary: <p>He’s no lawyer, but Wallace “Gator” Bradley was doing his best impression of one.</p><p>Bradley, a former Gangster Disciples enforcer who now calls himself an “urban translator,” was grilling murder exoneree Mark Maxson in a deposition in August over this $345,000 question:</p><p>Is Bradley owed a cut of Maxson's $8.75 million wrongful conviction settlement?</p><p>Bradley says he is.</p><p>Maxson disagrees. And he wasn't a friendly witness.</p><p>“Mark, were we considered like a team?” Bradley asked.</p><p>“No,” Maxson replied.</p><p>“I wasn't a part of a team that helped you?”</p><p>“No, not getting my freedom, no,” Maxson said. “My lawyers did.”</p><p>Bradley then pointed to a contract Maxson signed while serving a life sentence.</p><p>“What was the contract for?” Bradley asked.</p><p>“The contract was for you to be an urban translator,” Maxson answered.</p><p>Bradley pressed on: “When you signed the contract, you were really intending on paying me?”</p><p>“Yes,” Maxson said.</p><div ABC7</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>That exchange is now at the center of Bradley’s legal claim seeking payment for work he says he performed helping Maxson win his freedom.</p><p>Bradley says he logged 4,607 hours at $75 an hour — more than $345,000 — and has submitted about 70 pages describing the work he says he did between 2013 and 2015.</p><p>He listed dozens of City Council and Rainbow/PUSH Coalition meetings he says he attended, along with his preparation for those meetings. </p><p>He says there was outreach to the media and "community/political leadership”; a handful of meetings, emails and conversations with Maxson’s lawyers; and appearances at several events, including a 2023 Christmas party where Bradley says Maxson and Mayor Brandon Johnson also showed up.</p><p>Last month, a judge allowed the case to move forward on Bradley’s breach of contract claim, but denied two other counts — one for the value of his services outside the contract and another claiming Maxson’s attorneys violated an agreement to settle Bradley's claims.</p><p>A trial is scheduled in December.</p><p>“It’s his obligation to prove his case — and I don’t think he can do it,” Maxson’s lawyer, Jeffery Beck, said in an interview.</p><p>It’s not the first time Bradley has sought to get paid as an “urban translator.”</p><p>Bradley, who ran unsuccessfully for Chicago alderman in the 1990s and has remained a fixture at political events, began using the urban translator title after a federal judge allowed him to sit in court in 2006 and explain legal terminology to former death row inmate Aaron Patterson during his own wrongful conviction lawsuit against the city.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure JB Pritzker at a political event last year in downtown Chicago.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Bradley later sued Patterson for payment. Court records show they eventually settled the case for $75,000.</p><p>The dispute with Maxson stems from a 2013 contract with Bradley that Maxson signed while serving a prison sentence for the fatal stabbing and sexual assault of a 6-year-old boy.</p><p>Under the deal, Bradley was hired to provide “services [such] as media, community and political liaison to assist Maxson in gaining his freedom.”</p><p>Maxson, now 65, was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2016/10/4/18324360/wrongfully-convicted-man-mark-maxson-joins-21st-century" >freed in 2016</a> after DNA evidence tied the boy's killing to another man. In tossing out Maxson’s conviction, a Cook County judge said he’d seen “no greater tragedy” in his time on the bench.</p><p>Maxson <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2016/9/30/18364922/wrongfully-convicted-man-sues-city-for-54-million" >sued the city</a> for his wrongful conviction and in January 2025, the City Council voted to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/01/09/wrongful-conviction-8-75-million-chicago-police-mark-maxson" >pay him $8.75 million</a> for the more than 24 years he spent behind bars.</p><p>Bradley then attempted to get paid. Settlement negotiations with Maxson and his attorneys failed, leading to his current legal claims against Maxson in Cook County Circuit Court.</p><p>Maxson’s wrongful conviction saga began in 1992. He drew the attention of the Chicago police because he told a TV reporter he bought chips for Lindsey Murdock and told the first-grader to go home a day before he was found dead under debris in an abandoned garage near 107th Place and State Street.</p><p>Detectives said Maxson’s story kept changing. They accused him of beating, sexually assaulting and choking Lindsey, who also was stabbed with broken glass.</p><p>At his sentencing in 1994, Maxson told the court that detectives coerced his confession and that he was represented by incompetent public defenders. He also said the jury misunderstood the evidence.</p><p>“All of the evidence belonged to someone else,” he said at the time. “I am charged with a crime I did not commit.”</p><p>The judge, though, said Maxson, who had previously served prison time, was “malignant” and gave him a life sentence.</p><p>Then in 2015, Cook County State’s Attorney Anita Alvarez agreed to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2015/2/4/18431862/convicted-child-killer-to-get-dna-test-in-1992-case" >perform DNA tests</a> on the evidence in Maxson’s case. The DNA linked convicted killer Osborne Wade to the sexual assault and stabbing. Wade’s DNA was on Lindsey’s clothes.</p><p>Wade confessed and wrote letters to the boy’s family and Maxson apologizing, prosecutors said. Wade, now 52, pleaded guilty to a reduced charge of attempted murder in Lindsey’s killing and was sentenced to 50 years in prison.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/02/06/gangster-disciples-murder-wrongful-conviction-mark-maxson-wallace-gator-bradley" >‘Urban translator’ fighting for $312,000 slice of $8.75 million wrongful conviction settlement</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/01/09/wrongful-conviction-8-75-million-chicago-police-mark-maxson" >Wrongfully imprisoned for decades, Mark Maxson settles for $8.75 million</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2016/10/4/18324360/wrongfully-convicted-man-mark-maxson-joins-21st-century" >Wrongfully convicted man, Mark Maxson, joins 21st century</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

Michigan Ave.<br><b>When: </b>Through Dec. 19</p><p>Emmett Till was born 85 years ago, and this new photography exhibit asks the question: What if he had lived? What if Till had not been murdered in 1955 in Mississippi when visiting relatives from Chicago? The exhibit invites viewers to meditate on that question and the years stolen from Till by presenting a series of photographs that represent the life he might have had, from stills of neighborhood streets and playgrounds to Civil Rights-era photographs and shots of Michael Jordan and Barack Obama. The exhibit, curated by historian and scholar Sarah Elizabeth Lewis, in collaboration with the Rev. Wheeler Parker Jr., draws upon the museum’s permanent collection and features work by the likes of preeminent American photographers Dorothea Lange, Gordon Parks and Dawoud Bey.</p><div Wrightwood Ave.<br><b>When: </b>Through Dec. 19</p><p>Following her death in August in Tokyo, Chicagoans will have the chance to see works by Yayoi Kusama — including two of her immersive <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts/2026/09/24/yayoi-kusamas-infinity-mirror-rooms-wrightwood-659" target="_blank" ><u>Infinity Mirror Rooms</u></a>. The show at Wrightwood 659 includes nine works from the permanent collection of Washington, D.C.’s Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden. The exhibit presents Kusama alongside two of her art peers, Mary Bauermeister and Niki de Saint-Phalle. Each of the women was a trailblazer, building careers at a time when the art world was still overwhelmingly male-dominated, according to the show’s curator Betsy Johnson. In their own ways, Johnson said, the women shared a visual world that immersed the viewer in their art.</p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://www.artic.edu/exhibitions/10487/mary-cassatt-after-impressionism" target="_blank" ><b><u>Mary Cassatt: After Impressionism</u></b></a></h3><p><b>Where: </b>The Art Institute of Chicago, 111 S. Cottage Hill Ave., Elmhurst<br><b>When: </b>Through Jan. 3, 2027</p><p>This group show in suburban Elmhurst features all works created by veterans, who, according to the museum, “have turned away from militarism and toward solidarity.” The show features ceramics, sculpture, printmaking, photography and poetry, created by veteran artists examining their own military experiences and critiquing ongoing United States militarism. The display includes archival works from Vietnam Veterans Against the War and Iraq Veterans Against the War. The exhibit is part of the broader <a class="Link" href="https://resistingthelongwar.online/" target="_blank" ><u>2026 Veteran Art Triennial</u></a>, which will also include shows at the Chicago Cultural Center, Hyde Park Art Center and Walls Turned Sideways.</p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://art.org/exhibitions/karla-wong" target="_blank" ><b><u>Karla Wong: Journeys of Being</u></b></a></h3><p><b>Where: </b>Intuit Art Museum, 756 N. Milwaukee Ave.<br><b>When: </b>Through Jan. 10, 2027</p><p>Artist Karla Wong has called her work “a love letter to her Mexican culture,” which draws upon her own lived experiences and her identity as a trans woman. Born in Veracruz, Mexico, Wong has lived in Chicago for the past decade. Her work blends both her native Mexico and her adopted home of Chicago. In vibrant, colorful paintings, she features both traditional Oaxacan landscapes and clothing, as well as subtle nods to Chicago landmarks, like the Willis Tower. According to Intuit, Wong’s work evokes “Victorian and Surrealist styles” through “vivid, dreamlike compositions.”</p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://smartmuseum.uchicago.edu/exhibitions/teamlab-everything-exists-in-infinite-continuity" target="_blank" ><b><u>teamLab: Everything Exists in Infinite Continuity</u></b></a></h3><p><b>Where: </b>Smart Museum of Art, 5550 S. Greenwood Ave.<br><b>When: </b>Through Feb. 21, 2027</p><p>The Tokyo-based art collective teamLab makes its Midwest debut this fall in Hyde Park. The artworks explore the relationship between the self and the world through immersive, large-scale digital pieces. Since it was founded in 2001 by Toshiyuki Inoko, the group has grown to include hundreds of artists, scientists, computer programmers and mathematicians around the world. The show at the Smart Museum traces the group's origins and development over 25 years, featuring some of their most iconic artworks, as well as pieces made specifically for this exhibit.</p><div The Heckscher Museum of Art, Huntington, NY</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://driehausmuseum.org/exhibition/emma-stebbins-carving-out-history" target="_blank" ><b><u>Emma Stebbins: Carving Out History</u></b></a></h3><p><b>Where:</b> Driehaus Museum, 50 E. Erie St.<br><b>When: </b>Oct. 9-April 18, 2027</p><p>Emma Stebbins was widely celebrated as a leading sculptor during her lifetime in the 19th century. In 1873, she became the first woman commissioned by the city of New York to create a public sculpture, the result of which is the iconic Bethesda Fountain, which has a permanent home in Central Park (although it is currently undergoing a multimillion-dollar renovation). However, Stebbins’ place in art history has largely been forgotten in more recent years. Now, the first museum exhibition dedicated to Stebbins is coming to the Driehaus, as part of a touring show organized by the Heckscher Museum of Art in Huntington, New York. The show combines several of Stebbins’ neoclassical works, along with paintings and archival materials that contextualize her work. There is also a bust of Stebbins’ romantic partner, the renowned Shakespearean actress Charlotte Cushman.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> Halsted St.<br><b>When: </b>Through January 2028</p><p>As Christopher Nolan’s epic blockbuster commanded attention this summer, Chicago’s homegrown Greek history museum is diving deep into Homer’s enduring work with “The Odyssey Reimagined.” The exhibit features works from 16 contemporary artists who have reinterpreted the text’s themes across mediums like painting, sculpture, photography and textiles. The show is part of the museum’s broader “A Year with the Odyssey” program featuring film screenings, literary discussions and a community reading.</p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://nphm.org/exhibition/lydia-cheshewalla/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Lydia Cheshewalla: Our Stories, Like Roots in Soil</u></b></a></h3><p><b>Where:</b> National Public Housing Museum, 919 S. Ada St.<br><b>When: </b>Ongoing</p><p>The museum’s ongoing exhibit,“History Lessons: Everyday Objects from Public Housing,” recently added new objects with personal stories from members of the Osage Nation, including dance regalia, a 200-year-old beaver hat and a tie slide belonging to former Chief George Tallchief. The museum has also unveiled a newly commissioned installation by the Osage artist Lydia Cheshewalla, who used found materials gathered with the help of former public housing residents across the Jane Addams Homes site. The piece pulls together materials like used sparklers, pieces of tile and plants. Following its installation at the museum, Cheshewalla will return all natural materials to the place they were gathered, saying that the practice situates her work within the larger tradition of Indigenous land stewardship.</p><p><i>Courtney Kueppers is an arts and culture reporter at WBEZ.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-420000" name="module-420000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3><b>Your guide to fall culture in Chicago </b></h3><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-f6c56c02-ac5f-11f1-988e-bd5e5ce8e98f"><li>The next big thing is happening on Chicago’s small stages. <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/things-to-do/2026/09/04/theater-to-see-chicago-fall-storefront-tickets-new-plays-musicals" target="_blank" ><u>Here are 10 plays and musicals</u></a> not to miss this theater season.</li><li>The ultimate guide to <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/movies-tv/2026/09/10/chicago-fall-film-festivals-events-things-to-do-movies-ciff-cuff-reeling" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago’s fall film festivals</u></a>, from Oscar contenders to local standouts</li><li>Evanston’s $32 million <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/theater-stages/2026/09/03/evanston-northlight-theater-chicago-suburbs-arts-annex" target="_blank" ><u>new Northlight Theatre</u></a> wasn’t built for big crowds. It’s built for new plays.</li><li><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts/2026/09/08/mary-cassatt-after-impressionism-art-institute-chicago-paintings-impressionist-mural-worlds-fair-1893" target="_blank" ><u>“Mary Cassatt: After Impressionism”</u></a> is the Art Institute’s first deep-dive into Cassatt in more than 25 years and explores some of her historical Chicago ties.</li><li>There’s action in Chicago’s art galleries. entries.title: New Chicago History new exhibit features Mary Todd Lincoln’s blood-soaked cape and more
entries.summary: <p>Surrounded by a sea of sewing supplies, fabric and boxes, Michael Hall gently rolls out a slight mannequin, draped with an elegant black cape. Hall, whose job is to ready the mannequins for display, points to the garment’s bottom edge and says, “There are some splatters here.”</p><p>Those splatters, which will soon be on display inside the <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagohistory.org/exhibition/threads-of-a-nation-preserving-presidential-clothing/" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago History Museum</u></a>, represent the real and human cost of the infamous night when President Abraham Lincoln was assassinated at Ford’s Theatre and blood stained this dark velvet overcoat, reportedly worn that night by his wife, Mary Todd Lincoln.</p><div class="Enhancement FormEnhancement" data-align-center> <div id="Form-newsletter-wrapper" class="Form-newsletter-wrapper" data-module data-has-background ><a class="AnchorLink" target="_blank" >Privacy Policy</a></p> </div> </form> </bsp-form> </div> </div><p>The cape is a permanent but rarely displayed part of the museum’s vast textile collection of more than 50,000 items — essentially, the 19th-century equivalent of Jackie Kennedy’s blood-soaked pink suit. This month, it joins other Lincoln artifacts and clothing associated with the likes of George and Martha Washington and John Adams on display in a banner new exhibit at the Lincoln Park museum called “<a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagohistory.org/exhibition/threads-of-a-nation-preserving-presidential-clothing/" target="_blank" ><u>Threads of a Nation</u></a>.”</p><p>The exhibition, powered by a <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagohistory.org/chicago-history-museum-receives-grant-from-national-park-service-for-preservation-of-items-in-its-costume-collection/" target="_blank" ><u>Save America’s Treasures grant</u></a> of more than $450,000, focuses on presidential clothing and the extreme measures required to preserve these delicate pieces for generations of researchers and history lovers.</p><p>Visitors can see china from the Lincoln White House, dress fragments kept by Mrs. Lincoln's personal seamstress and a spyglass used by Washington. On view, too, are associated with both Washington and Lincoln.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-e40000" name="image-e40000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c99604e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fca%2Fe5%2F6ec516a0408981a19fbca44e292d%2Fpresidentialhistory-261006-007.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d45f180/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fca%2Fe5%2F6ec516a0408981a19fbca44e292d%2Fpresidentialhistory-261006-007.png 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/271884c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fca%2Fe5%2F6ec516a0408981a19fbca44e292d%2Fpresidentialhistory-261006-007.png" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Costume Mount Maker Michael Hall stands in his studio at the Chicago History Museum in Lincoln Park on the North Side, Thursday, Sept. 17, 2026. The museum team has ongoing investigations into the provenance of the historical items — many of which have been in the collection for decades — photographing them all thoroughly and taking precise measurements of the garments.</p><p>As Hall puts it, this is the team’s chance to extract as much information as possible before the items again enter a long stretch of dormancy.</p><p>Many of the pieces on view were acquired by the museum in 1920 from the prominent Chicago businessman Charles F. Gunther, a candy mogul, one-time alderman and enthusiastic collector, who ran a museum of his own before his death. “He had impeccable taste, and he had a lot of money,” said Jessica Pushor, collections manager at the history museum.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-380000" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>“Threads of a Nation” brings some of the museum’s more precious artifacts into view. It also underscores the effort of displaying centuries-old garments. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>In the late 1800s, Gunther bought 26 Lincoln relics from Elizabeth Keckly, a formerly enslaved woman who bought her freedom through her sewing skills and eventually worked as Mrs. Lincoln’s personal seamstress. In 1920, what was then known as the Chicago Historical Society purchased those items from Gunther’s estate, marking the beginning of the museum arm of the organization.  </p><p>On a rainy morning in mid-September, Hall and Pushor are in the throes of preparation, with about a month to go until the exhibit opens. As Hall puts it, this is the “hurry, hurry, hurry! Get it all done!” stretch.</p><p>Inside a shuttered exhibition space just off the museum's main lobby, Hall is hard at work constructing a replica of <a class="Link" href="https://images.chicagohistory.org/asset/34258/" target="_blank" ><u>a velvet suit Washington</u></a> is believed to have worn to his second inauguration.</p><div class="Enhancement" That one will be on display for the first half of the exhibit, along with Washington’s original suit coat, which, Hall says, “is maybe not in the best condition, and that's putting it lightly.”</p><p>Then, halfway through the show, the garments will be swapped. That original coat will be traded out for the original Washington vest, and the 1950s replica will be replaced by Hall’s new version. A brown velvet John Adams suit will also be swapped out for another that belonged to the second president, in a butter-yellow color.</p><p>The many wardrobe changes in the show underscore the push-and-pull felt by the museum team: They want to show the items off, but they also know that any amount of light exposure will degrade centuries-old fibers. “That's why you have to take them off exhibit and let them rest for a while,” Pushor said.</p><p>“Museums are trying to keep things for hundreds of years for an object that was not supposed to last that long,” Pushor added. “You're asking an object to last for years and years longer than it was supposed to.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>The many wardrobe changes in the show underscore the push-and-pull felt by the museum team: They want to show the items off, but they also know that any amount of light exposure will degrade centuries-old fibers. Here, is part of a suit reportedly worn by President John Adams.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>About 10 miles south, another curatorial team is grappling with how to preserve far more recent presidential garments. The newly opened Obama Presidential Center includes a display of clothing worn by former First Lady Michelle Obama on occasions like Election Night 2008 and the 2009 inauguration. But as museum director Louise Bernard told <a class="Link" href="https://www.instyle.com/inside-michelle-obamas-iconic-fashion-collection-at-the-obama-presidential-center-12014554" target="_blank" ><u>InStyle Magazine</u></a>, “We can only display these garments for 12 months before they have to rest for 10 years.”</p><p>While the Obama team has the benefit of living memory and color photographs to firmly trace the provenance of their collection (even still, well-known pieces like President Obama’s infamous tan suit <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/tansuit" target="_blank" ><u>have gone missing</u></a>), the history museum team is often trying to solve mysteries with few clues.</p><p>That velvet Washington suit? It’s purported that the first president wore it to his second inauguration, but historians also know that Washington had a few such suits in his wardrobe and can’t say for certain this is the one he donned while being sworn in.</p><p>As the team, led by guest curator Olivia Mahoney (who had a long tenure at the museum before switching to a freelance career) continues its provenance research, it must also provide caveats, clearly stating what it knows for certain — and what it’s still figuring out.</p><p>Pushor — who half jokingly quips her role at the museum can be summed up as: “If you can wear it, I take care of it” — is deep in research mode. Among the museum’s vast storage, she set out to find all 26 items that Elizabeth Keckly sold to Gunther from her time in the Lincolns’ realm. (Through research, Pushor has discovered that while Keckly’s name was often spelled “Keckley,” including on the cover of her memoir, she signed her own name as “Keckly,” which the history museum has opted to use.)</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-200000" name="image-200000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3522126/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F50%2F2f%2Fdb198c9e4256b0d55afcf5e8170b%2Fpresidentialhistory-261006-013.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/61041ad/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F50%2F2f%2Fdb198c9e4256b0d55afcf5e8170b%2Fpresidentialhistory-261006-013.png 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/781e5cd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F50%2F2f%2Fdb198c9e4256b0d55afcf5e8170b%2Fpresidentialhistory-261006-013.png" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Costume Mount Maker Michael Hall explains his process in studio at the Chicago History Museum in Lincoln Park on the North Side, Thursday, Sept. 17, 2026. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/781e5cd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F50%2F2f%2Fdb198c9e4256b0d55afcf5e8170b%2Fpresidentialhistory-261006-013.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/14450e7/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F50%2F2f%2Fdb198c9e4256b0d55afcf5e8170b%2Fpresidentialhistory-261006-013.png 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/781e5cd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F50%2F2f%2Fdb198c9e4256b0d55afcf5e8170b%2Fpresidentialhistory-261006-013.png" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Inside a shuttered exhibition space just off the museum’s main lobby, Hall is hard at work constructing a replica of a velvet suit Washington is believed to have worn to his second inauguration.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Pushor’s favorite discovery came one day when she was sorting through items with Mahoney and museum conservator Julie Benner. They unrolled a dress fragment and suddenly Pushor was overcome with what she was looking at: a piece of a dress Mary Todd Lincoln had worn to a wedding in 1861.</p><p>On that evening, the First Lady had her photo taken, a rare occasion for the time. While the black-and-white image remains, the dress itself is long lost, leaving historians to wonder about the garment’s color and fabric. Research for this exhibit led to the discovery of the dress fragment, saved by Keckly, which revealed a white silk fabric with purple dots and a multicolor floral brocade.</p><p>“It's just this full circle moment, and as a fashion historian, to know the color of the dots and everything and then, all of the information and provenance behind it, is just, to me, mind-blowing,” Pushor said.</p><p>Of course, the history museum is not the only Illinois institution interested in Lincoln artifacts. The Springfield-based Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum recently made headlines after a pair of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/illinois/2026/09/07/abraham-lincoln-bloodstained-gloves-assassination-california-museum" target="_blank" ><u>blood-stained gloves</u></a>, which were once envisioned to be part of the library’s permanent collection, resurfaced in Southern California after being sold at auction last year for $1.5 million.</p><p>The sale to a mystery buyer underscores that rare historical artifacts often have a hefty price tag and nonprofit institutions — many of which have faced financial hardships in recent years — aren’t always able to hold onto the items for the long haul. Plus, provenance research is time-consuming and expensive.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-3e0000" name="image-3e0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c9bea4d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F6d%2Ffe%2F27e1f5c4424ebf822431d689333f%2Fpresidentialhistory-261006-030.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/85e98f2/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F6d%2Ffe%2F27e1f5c4424ebf822431d689333f%2Fpresidentialhistory-261006-030.png 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/74121a6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F6d%2Ffe%2F27e1f5c4424ebf822431d689333f%2Fpresidentialhistory-261006-030.png" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="First Lady Mary Todd Lincoln’s cloak sits on mannequin in a mount making studio at the Chicago History Museum in Lincoln Park on the North Side, Thursday, Sept. 17, 2026. The cloak was worn the evening of President Lincoln’s assassination and its suspected that the splatter is his blood." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/74121a6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F6d%2Ffe%2F27e1f5c4424ebf822431d689333f%2Fpresidentialhistory-261006-030.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/344ddbe/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F6d%2Ffe%2F27e1f5c4424ebf822431d689333f%2Fpresidentialhistory-261006-030.png 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/74121a6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F6d%2Ffe%2F27e1f5c4424ebf822431d689333f%2Fpresidentialhistory-261006-030.png" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Curators can’t say definitively that the stains on Mrs. Lincoln’s black opera cape are President Lincoln’s blood. Being certain would require a DNA test, which would destroy a section of the garment.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Even at the history museum, where Mrs. Lincoln’s black opera cape will soon be on view, curators can’t say definitively that those stains are President Lincoln’s blood. Being certain would require a DNA test, which would destroy a section of the garment. And right now, the museum isn’t interested in that.</p><p>Instead, the team will make careful notes of what they know for sure and what they don’t. They'll share that with the public and invite them to make their own decisions, hoping that the chance to see these garments up close brings history to life for the viewers.</p><p>“When it comes to clothes or garments or textiles, these are things that are the closest you'll ever get to a person. So the sweat stains, oh yeah, that was their sweat that they put on it,” Hall said. “I think that's the importance of saving textiles; it allows us to glom onto what this person used to be like. It makes them more real.”</p><p><i>Courtney Kueppers is an arts and culture reporter at WBEZ. </i></p>

entries.title: Magic: The Gathering fans face shipping delays for new cards thanks to El Niño
entries.summary: <p>On a Saturday morning in September, the game shop Dice Dojo was packed. People were sitting arm-to-arm at tables lining the Edgewater store, opening Magic: The Gathering trading cards and playing in a tournament.</p><p>Noel Camilotas spent most of the day pacing past rows of packed tables and helping players decipher the rules of the hotly-anticipated new set release. But now, he was done for the day and walked out of the store with two boxes of cards.</p><p>Despite the armful of cards, Camilotas hoped for a bigger haul.</p><div class="Enhancement" href="https://magic.wizards.com/en/news/announcements/reality-fracture-play-booster-supply-may-be-tight-at-release" target="_blank" ><u>August</u></a> that its new set of Magic cards would be delayed throughout North America.</p><p>“Supply will be tighter at launch than anticipated as those boosters [card packs] make their way through the logjam,” according to the card game’s <a class="Link" href="https://magic.wizards.com/en/news/announcements/reality-fracture-play-booster-supply-may-be-tight-at-release" target="_blank" ><u>website</u></a>.</p><p>The company pointed to a drought-powered traffic jam at the Panama Canal, which facilitates nearly <a class="Link" href="https://pancanal.com/en/canal-de-panama-reafirma-su-papel-estrategico-y-su-agenda-de-sostenibilidad-en-inside-latam-panama-2025/" target="_blank" ><u>6% of global maritime trade</u></a> and about <a class="Link" href="https://www.fmc.gov/ftdo/statement-of-chairman-louis-e-sola-to-the-senate-committee-on-commerce-science-and-transportation-fees-and-foreign-influence-examining-the-panama-canal-and-its-impact-on-u-s-trade-and-n/" target="_blank" ><u>40% of US container traffic</u></a>. El Niño spikes surface water temperatures in parts of the Pacific Ocean, setting off extreme weather like floods and drought across the globe.</p><p>The delay is an early warning sign for how susceptible one of the world’s most important shipping lanes is ahead of what experts warn could be the strongest El Niño in history and a warming planet more generally.</p><div class="Enhancement" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Magic: The Gathering cards decorate a wall at Dice Dojo.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Magic: The Gathering has amassed more than <a class="Link" href="https://investor.hasbro.com/magic-gathering" target="_blank" ><u>50 million players</u></a> worldwide since its introduction back in 1993. The game has birthed an entire media ecosystem around it, as well as a robust resell market for rare cards. The rapper Post Malone reportedly purchased a one of a kind card based on the One Ring from a Lord of the Rings-themed set for <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2023/08/03/1191841285/post-malone-bought-magic-gathering-mtg-one-ring-card-million" target="_blank" ><u>$2 million dollars.</u></a></p><p>New card sets have been released every few months for years, allowing players to customize their decks endlessly. The model has been tremendously successful. Magic made its parent company Hasbro more than <a class="Link" href="https://investor.hasbro.com/news-releases/news-release-details/hasbro-reports-second-quarter-2026-financial-results" target="_blank" ><u>$1 billion</u></a> in revenue in just the first half of this year. Now, the trading card game is facing off with one of its greatest real-world foes yet: El Niño.</p><p>“The result of an El Niño for Central America is a very strong drought,” said Ross Griffith, the head of Americas freight pricing at Argus, a UK-based price-reporting agency. Parts of Panama received rainfall about 34% below the long-term average between May and August, raising concerns about water levels at the freshwater reservoir that powers the canal system and supplies drinking water to the region.</p><p>As a result, the Panama Canal Authority began restricting traffic, limiting daily crossing slots and driving up the bid prices shipping companies pay to secure a spot to cross. This isn’t the first time El Niño has slowed down traffic at the Panama Canal, daily crossings dropped down to 25 in November of 2023.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>People play Magic The Gathering at Dice Dojo. Fewer cards are getting through the Panama Canal because of an El Niño-powered drought.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>El Niño is expected to last into early 2027 and could stack on top of Panama’s upcoming dry season, according to Ross, who added that the delayed Magic cards could be just the beginning of more El Niño-induced traffic. “If you have drought conditions on top of a typically more dry period, even what little replenishment you were getting then is probably not coming,” he said. “That can be really dangerous.”</p><p>So, at least for now, card collectors in Chicago and beyond will likely be waiting longer than usual.</p><p>“Some products are now coming in waves,” Emma Hendren, the general manager at Dice Dojo said. “We're not going to have it available for sale today. We're not certain when it's going to arrive, unfortunately.”</p><p>Magic players are used to dealing with limited quantities or even delayed cards, but the ongoing climate change-powered hiccup is a new one.</p><p>“Magic the Gathering is all fantasy and all that stuff,” Joshua Wiltsie, who has been playing Magic for 30 years, said. “Even in our little corner of the multiverse, the supply chain affects us.”</p><p><i>This coverage is made possible through a partnership between WBEZ and </i><a class="Link" href="http://grist.org/" target="_blank" ><i>Grist</i></a><i>, a nonprofit environmental media organization.</i></p>

entries.title: What are the best tips for a first-time Chicago Marathon runner? Here's what you told us
entries.summary: <p>We asked readers for their tips for first-time runners of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-marathon" >Chicago Marathon</a>, which is on Sunday. Here's what you told us, lightly edited for clarity:</p><p>"Put your name on your shirt. People will scream it."<br><i>— Carol Cal</i></p><p>"Leave the headphones at home. Run near the curb and soak in the million people that want to scream support. ... It's not a race. It's a victory lap for all your hard work."<br><i>— Josh Mitzen</i></p><p>"Eat a lot of donuts the night before. You'll need the sugar."<br><i>— Dennis Sneyers</i></p><p>"Know what side of street your loved ones are on. Listen to the crowd, it’s electric."<br><i>— Kyle David</i></p><p>"Pick up your feet on the bridge. I have run in the race twice and both times tripped on the taped-down carpet going over the bridge in the first two miles."<br><i>— Jodie Lynne</i></p><p>"Just run like you practice in the neighborhood. Don’t focus on the other runners."<br><i>— Kenneth Leggin</i></p><p>"If you ever hit a moment of ‘I hate this, I want it to stop,’ just take it slower or walk and soak up how freaking incredible the accomplishment is."<br><i>— Meg Rog</i></p><p>"The finish line is broadcast on the TV news. Have someone record you."<br><i>— Linda Burrows</i></p><p>"Follow the painted tangent line as much as possible. Otherwise you’ll add up to another half mile before the finish."<br><i>— Josh Bass</i></p><p>"Avoid the Malört shots."<br><i>— Jenn MC</i></p><p>"When you go under the first tunnel, the guys use it as a urinal. Watch out for water stations, they get really slippery. Watch out for the crowd, they will walk in front of you just to get across the street."<br><i>— Lisa Kosobudzki</i></p><p>"Take an 800 mg ibuprofen at mile 15."<br><i>— Marcus Evans</i></p><p>"Wear a sweater in the morning that you’re willing to donate. It's cool early waiting at your corral."<br><i>— Luisa Salad-bar</i></p><p>"Bring some nutrition. I couldn't believe that they ran out of gels at the first aid station in 2024."<br><i>— Jason Bussell</i></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports/2026/10/06/2026-chicago-marathon-what-to-know-how-to-watch" >2026 Chicago Marathon — what to know, how to watch</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-marathon/why-runners-participate-history" >The Chicago Marathon is this weekend. >Obama Presidential Center workers to unionize</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydtjkujy-l-d/" target="_blank" >Ambar Colón</a></h5><p><b>Getting organized</b>: Obama Presidential Center workers are organizing a union, citing "increasing workload" and benefit rollbacks that have stirred concerns about their future with the organization. Workers plan to organize with the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees Council 31. Obama Workers United will represent more than 250 workers across the presidential center campus, at the Obama Foundation's offices in Washington, D.C., and remote workers.</p><p><b>Workers' POV</b>: In a letter signed by 68 workers and distributed to colleagues on Wednesday, employees allege that foundation leadership has met their concerns with "vague responses." The letter states the Obama Foundation and Obama Presidential Center have a "high turnover rate" and workers "continue to leave, taking with them their institutional knowledge and expertise."</p><p><b>Foundation response</b>: "We are deeply committed to the fundamental right of workers to organize and make their voices heard," an Obama Foundation spokesperson said in a statement to the Sun-Times and WBEZ.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: The 19.3-acre Obama Presidential Center campus opened to the public in June. The formation of Obama Workers United follows a major wave of Chicago museum and cultural workers unionizing, largely led by AFSCME Council 31.</p><p><a class="Link"
