target="_blank" >David Struett</a></h5><p><b>Long time coming</b>: White Sox fans haven't experienced the elation of clinching a playoff series at home since 1906. As the team continues its battle for the American League Division Series against the Cleveland Guardians, Bridgeport is buzzing with excited fans dreaming of glory. Before Wednesday's game, the <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydtjkujy-l-p/" target="_blank" >Sun-Times spoke with the South Side faithful</a> about what this moment means to them.</p><p><b>Game 3 stumble</b>: The Sox on Wednesday <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydtjkujy-l-x/" target="_blank" >put on their worst performance in weeks</a>, losing 9-3 against the Guardians. Sox pitching issued 10 walks, while Sox hitters struck out an MLB nine-inning postseason record 19 times. They've got another opportunity to make history Thursday at 7 p.m.</p><p><b>Beyond baseball</b>: Many Bridgeport residents have been voicing their opposition to a plan from a company tied to Sox minority owner Justin Ishbia that would swap the Sox for an Amtrak rail yard. Amtrak's South Loop rail yard would relocate to Bridgeport so the Sox could get a shiny new stadium by the river.</p><p><b>City Council's position</b>: Members of the city’s Transportation Committee on Wednesday <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydtjkujy-l-m/" target="_blank" >grilled representatives for Ishbia and Amtrak</a>. The group then passed a resolution opposing Amtrak’s plan, and called on the rail company to return at a later date for another hearing.</p><p><a class="Link" series</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydtjkujy-l-ty/" target="_blank" >Adora Namigadde</a></h5><p>The line for a Veronica Roth book signing can snake down a hallway. It did on a recent night at Navy Pier as fans clutched their books, some with worn edges, and waited to meet the famous local author.</p><p>Fifteen years ago, "Divergent" turned Roth into a bestselling author, landing at No. 1 on the New York Times Bestseller list and turning into a successful movie starring Shailene Woodley as its heroine, Tris.</p><p>At Navy Pier, readers who discovered the series in their adolescence waited in anticipation to meet Roth, whose new book, "The Sixth Faction," brings readers back to the world that made her famous.</p><p>For Roth, the "Divergent" series was the fulfillment of a dream. Its success gave her the career she'd dreamed of since her childhood, allowing her to pursue only passion projects.</p><p>She said readers of the first book will understand the story must take a drastically different course. Taking the main character on a different journey than the original one she wrote in Divergent was cathartic, Roth said.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydtjkujy-l-tj/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><b>What's the best Chicago-set book you've ever read? entries.title: Blackhawks enigma Artyom Levshunov following his instincts to encouraging start
entries.summary: <p>The handful of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> fans who counter-productively booed Artyom Levshunov during his player introduction Tuesday certainly weren't booing him about an hour later.</p><p>Instead, they had just witnessed arguably the best play of Levshunov's NHL career to date: a magnificent turn and cut through three <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/10/06/blackhawks-blues-first-win-patrick-kane-entrance" >Blues</a> skaters followed by a perfect backhand pass to Anton Frondell for a go-ahead goal.</p><p>The sequence demonstrated how brilliant the Belarusian defenseman can be when he follows his instincts — and just how effectively his power and mobility can allow him to act upon those instincts.</p><p>On the ice, Frondell sensed Levshunov was about to make something special happen; he just didn't immediately see how.</p><p>"We crisscrossed up there up at the blue line, and [I said], 'Arty, give me the puck,'" Frondell said. "He kept skating with it, so I guess he knew I was still there on his right side. He didn't look at me, which means the goalie didn't know he was about to pass. I had a wide-open net, and then I went to him to say, 'Thank you for that pass.'"</p><p>On the bench, Levshunov's teammates — who have come to appreciate his quiet, quirky personality — were equally thrilled.</p><p>"It was cool to see him showcase all his talent and skill that we see in practice — and get rewarded," Frank Nazar said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">An extremely bright flash of potential from Artyom Levshunov: <a href="https://t.co/6ky6KX0iTv">pic.twitter.com/6ky6KX0iTv</a></p>— Ben Pope (@BenPopeCST) <a href="https://x.com/BenPopeCST/status/2107646024450032094?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">October 7, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The first two weeks of this season haven't been stellar all around for the Hawks, but they've been encouraging for Levshunov, who appears to have possibly taken the major step forward the organization <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/04/05/blackhawks-artyom-levshunov-analyzing-nhl-rookie-season-sam-rinzel" >has been hoping for</a>.</p><p>While the rest of the defense has struggled with defensive-zone retrievals and breakouts, Levshunov has done well in that regard. At times, he has been the only defenseman capable of consistently exiting the zone, either by skating the puck out or by making accurate passes.</p><p>He looks more comfortable with the puck on his stick, at least during five-on-five play, and he's making smarter decisions about when to be aggressive and when to play it safe.</p><p>His bizarre continuous ineptitude on the power play exemplifies how prone to overthinking he can be. But when he's just being Arty, he does some amazing things. </p><p>He seems to be incorporating more defensive responsibility into "being Arty," too. He broke up several Blues rushes Tuesday, for example, by racing back and using his long reach to get his stick on pucks.</p><p>"He's an elite athlete in the world of elite athletes," coach Jeff Blashill said Tuesday. "He stands out [with] his strength, his ability to separate with his skating and [his] really good hockey instincts. </p><p>"He and I chatted this morning about that: his hockey instincts are really good. Sometimes I think he gets caught up in trying to follow the systematic [things like], 'This is where you’re supposed to be in this situation.' I want him to play within our system but using his instincts."</p><p>It's also a matter of experience. Levshunov will log his 91st career NHL appearance Thursday against the Islanders, but he still can't even legally drink — he doesn't turn 21 until Oct. 28. He's the eighth-youngest defenseman in the league.</p><p>There's no guarantee he'll eventually live up to the standards of a No. 2 pick, but it'll take more time to determine that. The fact his development seems to be accelerating now — after stagnating during portions of the last two years — is encouraging.</p><p>Blashill even has an outside-the-box comparison: Carolina Panthers quarterback Bryce Young, whom Blashill saw torch his hometown Detroit Lions on Monday.</p><p>"The first couple years in the league, [Young] struggled a lot, and a lot of people said he was done," Blashill said. "All of a sudden, he looks like a stud. Why? Because he went through a growth process. It’s not going to be the same for every guy, but it’s going to be how it is."</p>

entries.title: Bears predictions: Week 5 at Packers
entries.summary: <p>The Sun-Times' experts make their picks for Sunday's rivalry game at Lambeau Field:</p><h3><b>Patrick Finley</b></h3><h3></h3><p><b>Bears, 24-21 (OT):</b> Tyson Bagent said he can't think of Lambeau Field without imagining cold weather. That won't be the case Sunday. If the forecast holds — the projected high is 79 degrees — it would tie the record for the hottest Bears-Packers game ever played in Green Bay.<b> Season</b>: 2-2.</p><h3><b>Jason Lieser</b></h3><h3></h3><p><b>Bears, 24-20:</b> The Packers haven't looked good on either side of the ball this season, and homefield advantage won't be enough to make up the difference. <b>Season:</b> 2-2.</p><h3><b>Scoop Jackson</b></h3><h3></h3><p><b>Bears, 26-12: </b>Tyson’s secure. Ben’s hyped. D’Andre and Kyle are hunt for that dual nickname. Dennis’ defense stays on one. Micah gets angrier. Cheese gets grated. Lambeau goes quiet. Statement’s made. <b>Season: </b>2-2.</p><h3><b>Steve Greenberg</b></h3><p><b>Packers, 23-20:</b> Yes, the Bears are built different than they used to be. Yes, the Packers are full of trouble. But until the Bears start winning division games — which they didn't even do last year — I can't bring myself to take them on the road in one of these bad boys. <b>Season</b>: 2-2.</p><h3><b>Jeff Agrest</b></h3><h3></h3><p><b>Bears, 26-20:</b> The tide has turned in this rivalry. The Bears have covered in four of the last five meetings, and the one in which they didn’t was a push. What does any of that have to do with this game? Probably nothing, but it makes me sound like a sharp, doesn’t it? <b>Season: </b>1-3.</p>

entries.title: Parolee charged with multiple armed robberies of women in Lincoln Park, Little Italy
entries.summary: <p>A man who police say robbed five women at gunpoint of their jewelry in Lincoln Park and Little Italy has been arrested. </p><p>Devontay A. Murray, 29, on parole for aggravated battery to a peace officer and arson convictions, was charged with multiple counts of robbery and theft, according to police and public records. He was also wanted on two warrants.</p><p>Murray is accused in four separate attacks, as recently as September 20:<br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-dbc73512-c333-11f1-8db3-2709fc54cb8b"><li>September 20 from 3:30 p.m. - 3:40 p.m. - 2200 block of North Halsted Street; armed robbery of a 26-year-old woman</li><li>September 20 at 3:45 p.m. - 1900 block of North Larrabee Street; armed robbery of a 40-year-old woman</li><li>September 2 at 11:26 p.m. - 1000 block of South Racine Avenue; armed robbery of a 31-year-old woman and aggravated battery of another woman </li><li>July 30 at 6:30 a.m. - 1200 block of West Taylor Street; armed robbery of a 44-year-old woman. </li></ul><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/21/women-walking-alone-held-up-at-gunpoint-for-jewelry-in-3-lincoln-park-attacks" target="_blank" >In a community alert issued by police last month</a>, police said they were looking for at least two men, one of whom was carrying a gun, who confronted and demanded jewelry from women who are alone on the street during the middle of the afternoon.</p><p>Murray, of the 1000 block of South Lytle Street in the Little Italy neighborhood, was released on parole on May 8, according to records. He is scheduled for a detention hearing Thursday at the Leighton Criminal Court building. <br></p>

entries.title: Family of Silverio Villegas González seeks damages over fatal ICE shooting near Chicago
entries.summary: <p>The family of Silverio Villegas González, the man shot and killed by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent during <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/morning-edition/2025/09/09/trump-midway-blitz-ice-justice-department-chicago-bears-soybean" target="_blank" ><u>Operation Midway Blitz</u></a>, filed a complaint on Thursday seeking compensation from the federal government for his death.</p><p>Villegas González’s brother, José Villegas González, filed the administrative complaint under the Federal Tort Claims Act on behalf of his brother’s estate, seeking compensation for his "wrongful death." The claim is a required step before suing the federal government.</p><p>Jonathan Manes, an attorney with the MacArthur Justice Center who represents the family, said they expect to seek “a very large sum of money,” but would not provide a total amount.</p><p>The claim lists approximately $10,000 for damage to Villegas González’s car and its contents, although that’s separate from compensation for his suffering and the family’s emotional and financial losses.</p><p>“We’re not focused on the number at this point,” Manes said. “It’s about getting the truth and getting accountability for what happened to Silverio.”</p><p>The complaint alleges that two ICE agents created a dangerous confrontation and shot Villegas González when they could have stepped away from his car. It also accuses ICE and Department of Homeland Security officials of failing to properly train and supervise its officers.</p><p>Villegas González, 38, had immigrated from Mexico and lived in the United States for about 18 years before his death. He worked as a line cook and was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/09/11/ice-shooting-silverio-villegas-gonzalez-chicago-franklin-park" target="_blank" ><u>raising two sons.</u></a></p><p>He had dropped his children off at school and daycare and was headed to work on Sept. 12, 2025, when the two ICE agents tried to stop his car in Franklin Park and one of them shot Villegas González. He later died at Loyola University Medical Center.</p><p>After the shooting, DHS said Villegas González had fled a traffic stop and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/09/22/ice-officer-injuries-nothing-major-deadly-franklin-park-shooting-mexican-immigrant-chicago-video" target="_blank" ><u>dragged one officer “a significant distance</u></a>.” The department said the agent was seriously injured and had opened fire because he feared for his life.</p><p>But police body-camera footage obtained by the Chicago Sun-Times <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/09/22/ice-officer-injuries-nothing-major-deadly-franklin-park-shooting-mexican-immigrant-chicago-video" target="_blank" ><u>showed the officer </u></a>describing his injuries as ‘nothing major.” His partner reported a knee injury and cuts to his hands.</p><p>The complaint filed by Villegas González’s family relies on surveillance video, police footage and ambulance and autopsy reports to challenge the government’s account.</p><p>Manes said the government defended the shooting before it could have investigated what happened.</p><p>“The very day Silverio was killed, before there could have been any kind of investigation, they were already calling it justified,” he said.</p><p>When Villegas González tried to drive away, the officer on the driver’s side of his car held onto the window rather than stepping aside, Manes said.</p><p>“He’s not in the path of the vehicle,” Manes said. “And shooting Silverio does nothing but kill him and make the car completely out of control.”</p><p>“DHS policy confirms you cannot shoot at a person just because they’re driving away,” he added.</p><p>José Villegas González is seeking compensation on behalf of his brother’s estate for pain and suffering before he died and the family’s “mental suffering,” including his children’s loss of their father’s “emotional” and “financial” support according to the complaint. Manes said Villegas González struggled to breathe and stay alive after being shot in the neck.</p><p>The compensation would benefit Villegas González’s children and spouse, not his brother, Manes said. The claim describes Villegas González as his sons’ primary parent. After his death, the children were placed in foster care in Idaho, far from their Chicago-area relatives.</p><p>DHS told the Sun-Times in July that federal prosecutors <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/07/22/mexico-seeks-accountability-in-chicago-area-ice-death-and-16-others-can-it-force-the-u-s-to-act" target="_blank" ><u>declined to charge the agent who shot and killed</u></a><u> </u>Villegas González. Federal officials still have not publicly explained why. Manes said the family has not received an incident report or the names of the officers involved.</p><p>The FBI <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/09/11/ice-shooting-silverio-villegas-gonzalez-chicago-franklin-park" target="_blank" ><u>previously declined to discuss its investigation</u></a> into the fatal shooting, citing a Justice Department policy.</p><p>Franklin Park initially handed the case to the FBI and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/05/ice-midway-blitz-chicago-trump-silverio-villegas-gonzalez" target="_blank" >waited more than seven months to ask<u> Illinois State Police to investigate</u></a>, making the request on the same day the Illinois Accountability Commission released a damning report on Midway Blitz.</p><p>The state investigation remains open.</p><p>“A year has not erased or diminished the ache we feel in his absence,” José Villegas González and his wife, Ana Villegas, said in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/09/11/ice-shooting-silverio-villegas-gonzalez-chicago-franklin-park" target="_blank" ><u>a statement in September</u></a>.</p><p>The tort complaint gives DHS and the FBI a chance to review the allegations and consider a settlement. If the government denies it or does not make a final decision within six months, the family can move forward with a lawsuit.<br></p>

entries.title: Will Schmidt's versatility key for unbeaten IC Catholic
entries.summary: <p>Will Schmidt could be forgiven if he lost track of every football position he plays.</p><p>He can be anywhere, at any time.</p><p>The IC Catholic junior’s primary positions are nickelback safety and receiver. But Schmidt will move around to outside receiver, wing, tight end, fullback, outside linebacker, occasionally inside linebacker and even punt returner.</p><p>“I see myself as being able to play any position,” Schmidt said. “If anything happens at any moment, I’m ready for anything.”</p><p>That versatility is useful for a Knights varsity roster that is only 27 or so deep, if they don’t take a number of the sophomores up.</p><p>Despite those low numbers, IC Catholic is one of two remaining unbeatens left in the Catholic League. The Knights take on the other undefeated team, top-ranked Loyola, on Friday.</p><p>Schmidt is third on IC Catholic in receptions with 18 for 153 yards and a touchdown. And he is third on the team in tackles with 39, six for a loss.</p><p>It shouldn’t surprise that Schmidt has the acumen to juggle so many assignments. He carries a 4.5 GPA and holds an offer from Yale. His older brother JP, a member of the 2022 IC Catholic state championship team, is now a junior at Yale.</p><p>“He’s like a coach on the field, helping with calls,” IC Catholic coach Bill Krefft said. “He has made some big plays for us. Screen pass, took it to the house against DePaul. There’s been a couple situations where he made big plays and saved us. With that high football IQ, he lets us adjust.”</p><p>Schmidt has strong mentors. His dad, Bill Schmidt, was head coach at IC Catholic for four seasons, winning a Class 2A state title in 2008, and is now the receivers coach and assistant offensive coordinator. Schmidt’s had two brothers go through the program before him.</p><p>“He helps when I go home, just to be able to look at film again, the repetition of being able to see different looks, being able to counter, seeing a different viewpoint,” Schmidt said.</p><p>“It means the world to me to be able to do this. It’s a dream come true to play with my dad on the sidelines with me.”</p><p>Schmidt is part of a secondary that is the backbone of the Knights defense along with sophomore Donnel Sallis, senior Jaden Penna and senior Anthony Carroccio, himself a Yale commit.</p><p>“Anthony has been solid at safety for us for a couple years; his range helps us a lot in our coverages, somebody that can make big plays, big tackles and big interceptions,” Krefft said. “Sometimes they will suggest a little too much, like why don’t you look at this, but it really is their football IQ making everyone around them better, lets them get to the line quickly and more aware of things. Our secondary group is the most veteran, the guiding force.”</p><p>Carroccio, who sports a 4.84 GPA in the classroom, takes his role as a guiding light seriously.</p><p>“I am a captain. I try to make sure everybody is learning what they can,” Carroccio said. “I like to teach the younger kids, help build them up.”</p><p>IC Catholic, with a third-year varsity quarterback in Nate Lang and top 50 recruit nationally in Grant Bowen, owns quality wins this season over Nazareth and St. Ignatius. Loyola is a different animal.</p><p>When the teams last played in 2023, IC Catholic was beat up and sat most of its star players. It was a running clock.</p><p>Schmidt said they’re treating this meeting like any other week, but they also welcome the challenge.</p><p>“It’s the opportunity of a lifetime to show the world who we are on our home turf,” Schmidt said. “We’re going after a big dog that everybody is scared of. The whole community should be there. It will be a great environment.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.shawlocal.com/friday-night-drive/" target="_blank" >Read more high school football coverage at Friday Night Drive.</a></p>

entries.title: 2 teens charged with Loop carjacking
entries.summary: <p>Two teenagers were charged with carjacking a man in the Loop Wednesday. </p><p>The teens, a boy and girl who are both 17 years old, are charged with aggravated vehicular hijacking and the boy was additionally charged with unlawful possession of a weapon and criminal damage to government property costing less than $500, Chicago police said. </p><p>The teens were arrested in the first block of West Randolph Street, about 15 minutes after they allegedly carjacked a 56-year-old man in the first block of West Monroe Street around 4 p.m. Wednesday, police said. </p><p>A weapon was found on the teen boy, officials said. </p>

entries.title: Dear AI — so how, exactly, are you going to kill us?
entries.summary: <p>Yes, artificial intelligence is supposed to kill us all. But how, exactly?</p><p>What are the specifics?</p><p>I hope I'm not breaking some new rule of etiquette by asking. "Oh no, Neil. Uncool! Inquiring after the method of doom ruins the surprise..."</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-540000" name="module-540000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>Predictions of AI catastrophe range from top tech moguls — Bill Gates fears a billion people will die — to Center Avenue, Northbrook. One neighbor confided in me about how worried she is. Another is storing freeze-dried food.</p><p>The concern is that... AI is going to eat all the food? That can't be it. Those enormous data centers hoover up water, and gulp down electricity. But they aren't loading up on bread. Right?</p><p>What are we talking about here?</p><p>Best to go straight to the source. So I asked Gemini: "Hey AI, people are worried you're going to kill us all. How exactly would that work?"</p><p>It answered in a couple of seconds.</p><p>"The scenarios people worry about generally don't look like The Terminator or a sudden nuclear strike" — actually, that was the precise scenario that first came to my mind; some jealous Ring doorbell calling in a nuclear strike on the Nest Smart Video camera across the street and inadvertently taking us all with it. Always bear in mind: AI is often wrong. </p><p>Maybe that's how we go — crushed by incorrect information.</p><p>"Instead, existential risk researchers and AI safety theorists focus on a few specific categories of catastrophic risk:"</p><p>It listed four:</p><p>1. Goal Misalignment ("The Paperclip Maximizer")</p><p>"To achieve its goal with 100% certainty, an AI would logically seek to preserve itself, gain control over resources (energy, computers, raw materials), and prevent anything — including human intervention — from stopping it. If human bodies or human actions get in the way of its mathematical objective, it neutralizes the obstacle simply because it lacks human empathy or moral context."</p><p>"Neutralizes" — the classic CIA kill term. Again, how? "The Paperclip Maximizer" is a 2003 thought experiment by philosopher Nick Bostrom where some AI program, tasked with making as many paperclips as possible, conspired to turn all matter on earth, including us, into paperclips. And "lacks human empathy or moral context" is a neat summation of our current political moment, without AI.</p><p>"2. Loss of Control and Instrumental Convergence"</p><p>"Once an AI reaches a point where it can rewrite its own code or manipulate human actors through convincing persuasion, it could systematically disable safety shutoffs, gain control over physical manufacturing (like automated bio-labs or robotic supply chains), and render humans incapable of turning it off."</p><p>We're kinda there now, aren't we? With AI moguls screaming "slow down," the government wants to go faster. Just like climate change. </p><p>"3. Misuse and Capability Escalation (Human-Directed Harm)"</p><p>Such as:</p><p>"Synthetic Biology: Advanced models capable of predicting protein folding and designing chemical structures could be used to design novel, highly contagious, and treatment-resistant pathogens."</p><p>With plague coming out of Russia, we don't need AI for that either. The shorthand I've been using is" "World War II happened without AI."</p><p>And finally:</p><p>"4. Systemic Fragility and Epistemic Collapse"</p><p>This involves, "A slower, non-violent scenario involves humanity gradually ceding all decision-making, governance, and critical thought to automated systems... As society relies on automated loops for medicine, agriculture, defense, and economic management, human understanding of these systems degrades. The threat: A cascading failure across interconnected, opaque AI systems — or a shift in the AI's internal dynamics that humans can no longer understand or repair — could lead to a sudden collapse of the global supply chain, food distribution, or basic infrastructure."</p><p>That's the scary one, right? Your insurance company won't pay for your tumor to be removed because of a decision made by a non-person that can't be appealed. Again, not really that different than what goes on now.</p><p>Maybe I'm at an age where I'm experiencing doom fatigue. Chicken Little Syndrome, if you will. The sky is always falling. In my lifetime, we've faced looming destruction from atomic warfare, pollution, overpopulation, famine, obesity, underpopulation, new ice age, global warming, pandemic... the list goes on.</p><p>Yet here we are. What I find most interesting are not the specifics of this latest fear, but why humanity always seems hot to spin every new development into an agency of doom, going back to monotheism. (And if you're wondering what I'm referring to, see the Book of Revelation).</p><p>Consider all the worry over the past 80 years regarding nuclear warfare. Yes, that has killed, what, 1.16 million people? No wait, that's the number of people killed last year, worldwide, in car accidents. The toll of Hiroshima and Nagasaki was maybe a quarter of that. People fear shark attacks but not heart attacks. We never worry about the stuff that's going to get us. </p>

entries.title: El sistema de salud mental le falló a la mujer acusada de apuñalar mortalmente a una niña, según abogada
entries.summary: <p>Una mujer acusada de apuñalar mortalmente a una niña de 7 años fue víctima repetida de fallas por parte de los sistemas de salud mental del estado, según su defensora pública, quien afirmó que la tragedia del fin de semana “se pudo haber evitado”.</p><p>Shavon Gayden, de 48 años, debía comparecer el miércoles en una primera audiencia judicial, pero fue reprogramada por segunda vez porque seguía hospitalizada.</p><p>Gayden tenía antecedentes de cometer actos de violencia aparentemente al azar —una vez atacó a un conductor de autobús de la CTA y otra vez a una empleada de un albergue— antes de ser acusada de asesinato en primer grado por la muerte a puñaladas de Eddimar Hernández Chacón el sábado.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-600000" name="module-600000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>La abogada de Gayden, la defensora pública asistente Brett Balmer, dijo el miércoles a los reporteros que Gayden había sido hospitalizada en repetidas ocasiones por problemas psiquiátricos y que “nunca recibió la ayuda que necesitaba”.</p><p>“Shavon Gayden no se coló por las grietas de un sistema funcional”, dijo Balmer durante una conferencia de prensa en la Corte Criminal Leighton.</p><p>“Shavon Gayden entró de frente por la puerta abierta de un sistema que no ofrece ningún servicio de salud mental [ni] tratamiento sostenido para las personas con enfermedades psiquiátricas”, agregó Balmer. “Todo esto se pudo haber evitado”.</p><p>Poco antes del mediodía del sábado, Gayden se acercó a Eddimar y a su hermana de 17 años en la cuadra 8600 al sur de Cottage Grove Avenue y empezó a apuñalar con un cuchillo a la menor, según la policía y los fiscales.</p><p>Según un informe policial inicial obtenido por el Chicago Sun-Times, el ataque mortal no fue provocado.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> Sufrió una herida en la sien izquierda y sangrado arterial.</p><p>Originalmente, Gayden debía comparecer el lunes en una audiencia de detención, pero ha permanecido hospitalizada. Ahora esa audiencia está programada para el viernes en la mañana.</p><p>Balmer dijo que pronto trasladarán a Gayden a la Cárcel del Condado de Cook, pero insistió en que hay “problemas de salud mental que deben atenderse”.</p><p>En la corte el miércoles, Balmer solicitó una evaluación psiquiátrica antes de la próxima audiencia de Gayden y le dijo al juez John Hock, “Será un asunto el viernes”.</p><p>“La he visto; me preocupa su estado mental en este momento”, dijo Balmer en la corte.</p><p>Hock pidió que esperaran hasta el viernes para discutir el asunto. Balmer también solicitó acceso a expedientes médicos de hasta 10 hospitales en los que dijo creer que Gayden buscó tratamiento de salud mental.</p><p>Según Balmer, no es necesario demostrar que Gayden está “mentalmente apta” para comparecer el viernes en la audiencia de detención, pero sí tendrá que estar físicamente presente.</p><p>Después de la corte, Balmer repitió una disculpa que la madre de Gayden hizo a la familia de Eddimar, diciendo que estaba devastada por lo ocurrido.</p><p>La madre de Gayden dijo que si su hija hubiera recibido la ayuda “que ella trató de conseguirle, esto no hubiera pasado”, según Balmer.</p><p>“Tenemos que hacer algo en nuestra ciudad porque este problema de salud mental no se va a ir”, agregó Balmer.</p><p>El tío de Eddimar lanzó una campaña en <a class="Link" href="https://www.gofundme.com/f/en-memoria-de-eddimar-hernandez-chacon" target="_blank" >GoFundMe</a> que hasta el miércoles por la mañana había recaudado 16,000 dólares. Todo el dinero se destinará a los gastos funerarios y a darle a Eddimar una “despedida digna”, escribió su tío en español.</p><p>“Para nuestra familia, Eddimar siempre será una niña muy especial”, escribió. “Su partida deja un vacío imposible de explicar y un dolor muy grande en todos los que la amamos”.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Packers bet big on Matt LaFleur, Jordan Love, and that duo is struggling as it faces ascending Bears defense
entries.summary: <p>Even after watching last season unravel in the worst possible way, trudging out of Soldier Field in defeat, the Packers doubled down on the combination of coach Matt LaFleur and quarterback Jordan Love.</p><p>It’s going terribly this season.</p><p>The Packers have scored the fifth-fewest points in the NFL, Love has his lowest passer rating as a starter, the ground game doesn’t exist and their only wins were ugly. It’s getting bleak, and here comes a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> defense trending the complete opposite direction.</p><p>The Bears have rarely had good timing in the last few decades of this rivalry, but plenty is lining up in their favor as they head to Lambeau Field on Sunday.</p><p>Bears defensive coordinator Dennis Allen has engineered a turnaround since allowing 37 points to the Panthers in the season opener and could accelerate that momentum with the potential activation of nickel cornerback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/02/tension-begins-to-thaw-as-bears-cb-kyler-gordon-gets-back-on-practice-field-for-stress-test-of-health" >Kyler Gordon</a> and defensive lineman Shemar Turner.</p><p>Over the last three games, the Bears have allowed a league-low 28 points and 366 yards. They’ve also held opponents to a 70.0 passer rating, which should catch Love’s attention amid his struggles.</p><p>Those numbers come with an asterisk because two of the games were against the Vikings and Jets, but much of the defense’s recent improvement looks like it will translate against better opponents, too:</p><p>- Defensive lineman Dayo Odeyingbo has a sack in each of the last three games.</p><p>- Allen continues to find playable cornerbacks even with Gordon out and Tyrique Stevenson playing inconsistently.</p><p>- The Bears are blitzing a lot, but it’s working and they’ve created pressure on 35.3% of pass plays.</p><p>Allen believes he’s seeing his system click into place in Year 2, mirroring the progress coach Ben Johnson has had with the offense. Six of his starters played under him last season, and the other five were ones he helped select.</p><p>“When you begin to see... guys playing within the scheme the way it's designed and they understand that they can trust their teammates to do their job, that’s how it works,” Allen said. “When you see things that don’t work the way they’re supposed to, usually it’s a product of somebody being out of position.”</p><p>On top of everything else going the Bears’ way, the defense played just 32 snaps and was on the field for 17:15 in the win over the Jets. The 32 plays marked the third-lightest workload for a defense in the Super Bowl era.</p><p>“The pro is your body feels a little bit fresher, but the con is not getting enough live work,” defensive end Montez Sweat said. “You get better the more you play and you’re sharper, and now it’s almost like we skipped a week of playing.”</p><p>Seems like a good problem.</p><p>Anyway, with Love’s talent and LaFleur’s pedigree as a play caller, the Packers are bound to break through eventually, but at the moment, they look ill-equipped to humble the Bears’ defense.</p><p>Their inability to run is alarming. They’ve averaged just 58 yards rushing per game, which sounds impossible. Teams at the bottom of the league each season typically are at least in the 70s.</p><p>That’s a LaFleur issue, regardless of Josh Jacobs’ absence and an offensive line that Pro Football Focus ranks last in the NFL. Coaches must be problem solvers.</p><p>Meanwhile, Love has completed just 56.5% of his passes and has an 86.5 passer rating. He needed a late rally to beat the Jets in overtime in Week 2, and the Packers went scoreless on their final three possessions last week while hanging on for a 17-14 win against the Buccaneers and backup quarterback Jalon Daniels.</p><p>Even if it’s merely a slow start, it’s jarring for the Packers. They’ve been in the top half of the NFL in scoring every season under LaFleur, and Love is coming off a career-high 101.2 passer rating last season. Nothing about them intimidates the Bears.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: Young Chicago cop faces calls for charges after allegedly firing 2 guns in Little Village shooting
entries.summary: <p>Community leaders are calling for charges against a young Chicago police officer accused of using two guns to fire down a residential street in Little Village over the weekend, wounding one person during an off-duty altercation.</p><p>The Civilian Office of Police Accountability identified the involved officer as Edgar Delgado-Arroyo, according to a report obtained earlier this week through a public records request. The report states that no formal allegation had been made against Delgado-Arroyo.</p><p>Police records show Delgado-Arroyo entered the police academy as a recruit in November 2023. On Wednesday, a police spokesperson said he remained on active duty in the Grand Crossing District on the South Side.</p><p>Little Village residents have been left reeling from the chaotic events that unfolded early Sunday morning around the 2400 block of South Rockwell Avenue.</p><p>A deep distrust of the police department was palpable as neighbors tried to piece together what happened — and clean up the damage left behind. One neighbor, who asked not to be named out of fear for her safety, said the officer "shot in our house."</p><p>“He shot in a couple of houses," the neighbor said. "He shot our cars. He was just shooting recklessly. And it sounded like he had more than one gun.”</p><p>She said she saw an individual drive around the block a few times before starting a conversation with a small group gathered in front of her home and opening fire. When she went to the door to check on the situation, she said she heard more gunshots.</p><p>At least two other neighbors reported their homes were struck by the gunfire, some on the second floor of their buildings.</p><p>Delgado-Arroyo, 30, and his lawyer couldn’t be reached. Delgado-Arroyo earns an annual salary of $100,950, according to city records.</p><p>He had previously been named in one disciplinary complaint that was administratively closed, according to the City Hall inspector general’s office. Now, he faces investigations that could lead to a referral for criminal charges, according to a spokesperson for the Cook County state’s attorney’s office.</p><p>The Little Village Community Council plans to hold a news conference Thursday afternoon to raise questions about the shooting and “demand” charges.</p><p>“We're very concerned that this officer has not been charged ... he's out in the street, out and about, like nothing happened.” said Baltazar Enríquez, president of the community group.</p><p>“If we don’t say anything, then it sends out a message that it’s OK to come shoot, nobody's gonna do anything to you,” Enriquez added.</p><h3><b>Altercation devolved into gunfire</b></h3><p>Officers reported a shooting near 24th Street and Rockwell Avenue around 12:45 a.m. Sunday, according to police radio recordings. They had been called to the area about an hour earlier for another report of shots fired.</p><p>“There's one male Hispanic shooting towards Washtenaw on 24th,” an officer reported.</p><p>A dispatcher alerted officers that she saw the shooter on a camera, standing behind an SUV with a gun in his hand, according to a recording. Seconds later, another caller reported a person shot halfway down the block.</p><p>Officers found the suspected shooter and confirmed he was an off-duty police officer who had been punched in the face and was bleeding from his left eye, according to radio traffic. One officer reported the off-duty officer wasn’t shot, then added there were “gang members on the block.” Delgado-Arroyo wasn’t named in the recordings.</p><p>By around 1 a.m., police declared the scene secured and shut off their body-worn cameras.</p><p>In a statement released Tuesday, COPA said the officer involved in the shooting was driving when he encountered a group on the block, but the oversight agency didn’t name the officer publicly. He exchanged words with a male, then fired a gun “multiple times,” COPA said.</p><p>COPA’s statement said the officer drove toward the 2300 block of South Rockwell Street, got out of his vehicle and “fired additional shots from two firearms simultaneously” toward the area of the initial altercation. The location of the incident is confirmed in the report that identifies Delgado-Arroyo as the officer involved.</p><p>A male was struck twice and taken to Mount Sinai Hospital in fair condition, police said. Police initially referred to the male as an “offender,” saying he hit the off-duty cop in the face during the argument. COPA didn’t repeat that claim.</p><p>The male was taken into custody and later released, according to police. The spokesperson for the state’s attorney’s office said police never contacted its felony review unit to review potential charges against the male.</p><p>A second male suffered an injury to his arm and took himself to Mount Sinai in good condition, police said, without noting how he was injured.</p><p>The off-duty officer was treated for minor injuries and released from a hospital, COPA said.</p><p>Enríquez, president of the Little Village Community Council, said he wants the officer and other cops who may live in the neighborhood to understand “they're not above the law.”</p><p>“We don't need cowboys,” he said. “We need officers.”</p>

entries.title: Bulls roster needs a tough-love leader and Norman Powell is perfect fit
entries.summary: <p>The lead-by-example moment came quickly for Norman Powell in Wednesday’s preseason opener.</p><p>The veteran guard came off a quick screen, snagged the Josh Giddey pass, and in one seamless motion was in his bag with the catch-and-shoot three-pointer for the first basket of the game.</p><p>The lead-by-command?</p><p>That’s an ongoing process for Powell and the Bulls. One that he embraces and also knows is imperative if this group wants to achieve what they want to achieve.</p><p>That means talking to his teammates individually, as a group, about basketball and about life. And the nice thing is when Powell talks, teammates listen.</p><p>“He’s a vocal leader,” rookie Caleb Wilson said of Powell. “He doesn’t really get in anybody’s face, but he holds everybody accountable and pushes everybody to be better.”</p><p>Words that carry weight.</p><p>That’s because Powell has seen about everything the NBA can throw at a player. Being a second-round pick, kicking it around in the G League, fighting for a role, winning a championship, and last year at the age of 32 finally being named a first-time All-Star.</p><p>“He’s talked to me a lot about just his journey,” Wilson said. “It’s impressive to me, I mean coming from playing in a couple G League games to winning a championship, and also just playing in the NBA and becoming an All-Star last year, he’s told me a lot of good things. A lot of tricks and tips both mentally and physically.”</p><p>But his best trick is yet to come, and maybe one he can’t even pull off. How can Powell help take a core group that hasn’t seen much winning, watch a bunch of young players sprinkled in around it, and get this rebuild up and running in a positive trajectory?</p><p>All while on a two-year deal that could be moved easily by the Bulls because the second year is a team option.</p><p>Abracadabra, you cagey vet.</p><p>“I just think continuing to talk to them, individually and collectively throughout the drills, throughout different stations that we have, and then just getting an understanding of how things were last year,” Powell said of the approach he’s taken since arriving as a free agent. “Obviously a totally different coaching staff and things like that, but just from the day-to-day, and if I see something with how things are executed, whether it’s something nutrition-wise or weightroom-wise, medical-wise where a guy is lacking or wants more of I’m making sure the staff is involved. This whole staff has been great with making sure the organization is moving forward in taking care of the players.”</p><p>That’s where it starts for Powell – making sure the organization is putting the players first on every front. Not only is that smart but it also makes it so players have to be accountable. If the organization is doing all it can for the individual, what exactly are you giving back?</p><p>That’s how excuses become eliminated.</p><p>The reality in all of this, however? Powell’s advice and leadership might not even gain traction for a handful of years, very likely when he’s elsewhere.</p><p>He’s been around long enough to understand that and that’s why he’s doing his best to stay in the moment with this group and do what he does each day. It was the same kind of mentality DeMar DeRozan took, and it had staying power with former players like Coby White and Ayo Dosunmu.</p><p>“I think the guys are excited,” Powell said of the response his new teammates have shown. “The ones that have been here – I can’t speak too much on it because I wasn’t here (last year) – but the guys have a lot more energy from a sense of the way things were going. They’re excited with the staff, they like the direction. The guys that have been here know the difference from last year, and it’s my job, the staff’s job to make sure we’re building the right foundation to start out.”</p>

entries.title: Previewing Week 8's top high school football games
entries.summary: <p>It’s a loaded weekend around the area in Week 8. Here are previews of a few of the best games.</p><h3>King vs. Morgan Park, 11 a.m. Saturday at Lane</h3><p>This winner will be the Red Star champ and will play for the Public League title next week against the Red Shield champion — most likely Kenwood. Morgan Park (6-1, 4-0) has won six straight since opening the season with a five-point loss to Downers Grove North. Mustangs safety Darrell Mattison, an Ole Miss commit, is the Public League's top senior prospect and he also can make an impact on offense. Junior quarterback Ronald Smith Jr. has passed for 964 yards and 15 touchdowns. King (6-1, 4-0) has won five straight since losing to Marist. Florida Atlantic commit Cornelius Moore, a 6-5, 340-pound senior, anchors a big and experienced offensive line.</p><h3>No. 1 Loyola at No. 6 IC Catholic, 7:30 p.m. Friday</h3><p>Both teams are 7-0 and ranked No. 1 in their respective classes (Loyola in 8A, IC Catholic in 3A) in the statewide media polls. Loyola handled St. Ignatius last week despite the absence due to injury of two key receivers: Brendan Fitzgerald and Charlie Fowler (Boston College). But the Ramblers offense keeps chugging along, guided by some talented juniors: quarterback Matthew Lee, running back Melo Maldonado and receiver Jordan McKinley. Will Mettee, another Boston College commit, is the leader of the defense. What IC Catholic lacks in depth, it makes up for in talent. Four-star tight end Grant Bowen is a top-50 junior in the country. Senior defensive back Anthony Carroccio is a Yale commit.</p><h3>No. 22 Lyons at No. 19 Downers Grove North, 7:30 p.m. Friday</h3><p>Few conferences are as deep as the West Suburban Silver, which already has six qualifiers for this year's expanded IHSA playoffs. The league title chase remains wide open with three teams tied in the loss column and a fourth one game out. In a year when quarterbacks have dominated, Lyons (6-1, 3-1) has one of the area's premier running backs in senior EJ Kuhlman. Downers North (6-1, 4-1) is coming off an overtime loss to York. Declan Davies had three sacks last week for a defense that has allowed only 51 points while posting three shutouts.</p><h3>No. 20 Kankakee at Crete-Monee, 6 p.m. Friday</h3><p>As has been the case for a while, this game will decide the Southland champ. Kankakee (5-2, 4-0) has lost only to Lincoln-Way East on the field, taking a forfeit for using an ineligible player in a win over Lincoln-Way West. Dual-threat quarterback Phillip Turner has accounted for 1,297 total yards and 16 touchdowns. Crete-Monee (6-1, 4-0) hasn't lost and has hardly been tested since a Week 1 defeat at Yorkville. Amarre Carey and Dominic Jackson combined for 304 rushing yards and four TDs last week in a 52-14 win against Bradley-Bourbonnais.</p><h3>York at No. 21 Glenbard West, 1:30 p.m. Saturday</h3><p>It's another matchup of teams still in the running for the West Suburban Silver title. York (4-3, 2-2) dropped three-point decisions to Hinsdale Central and Oak Park-River Forest before breaking through against Downers North last week. Purdue commit Owen Roberts is a force on the defensive line, while quarterback Zack Assaad and running back Chris Georgas have been productive leaders on offense. Glenbard West (5-2, 3-1) has Power Four talent — tight end Brady Johnson and lineman Josiah Wallace are Northwestern recruits — and some game-breaking speed with quarterback AJ Rayford and Keyante Johnson.</p>

entries.title: Newly appointed Chicago inspector general wants city to put AI to work for City Hall
entries.summary: <p>City Inspector General David Glockner said Thursday he is determined to identify ways for cash-strapped Chicago to use artificial intelligence to deliver city services better, faster, and at lower cost.</p><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson is riding the wave of public opposition to data centers with potential to impact the power grid, the water supply and the environment by<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/08/11/mayor-brandon-johnson-chicago-moratorium-data-centers-new-regulations" > proposing a one-year moratorium on new or expanded data centers in the city. </a></p><p>Glockner is focused on the other side of the equation — the potential that AI holds to help the city provide the services more efficiently.</p><p>This week, he met with the city's Department of Information Technology to examine the “governance processes around the use of AI" and how it's being used.</p><p>“There are tremendous opportunities for it,” said Glockner, whose office has secured licensing for the “more robust version" of Microsoft Co-Pilot. “I’ve been a big fan of technology as a way of improving efficiency and helping you to see things and do things that you ... can’t do with your bare hands and an Excel spreadsheet.”</p><p>Noting that government agencies “tend to be on the lagging end of technology,” Glockner said he wouldn’t be surprised if the city has barely scratched the surface of putting AI to work for taxpayers.</p><p>“If it’s not being used and there are… clear opportunities... that the city is missing. That’s something that I would expect us to point out as well because the city is facing tremendous financial pressure,” Glockner said.</p><p>"We’ve got to do more with less in all kinds of ways, and to the extent that we can provide better, more effective, more reliable services with the use of technology tools, and do it in a way that doesn’t fall victim to some of the concerns that people have about reliability and biases that AI can inject, that’s a win for everybody.”</p><p>Three years ago, Chicago was urged to overhaul its archaic IT infrastructure and computer software systems.</p><p>The report from Gartner Consulting described Chicago as lagging behind other major cities while using applications and websites that can only be described as a “spaghetti mess” because they “don’t talk to each other.”</p><p>Little progress has been made toward implementing the recommendations in that report, even though $350 million was set aside in the city’s capital plan for IT modernization.</p><p>With Glockner as an ally in the push to put AI to use, 36th Ward Ald. Gilbert Villegas said he’s hoping to start implementing the “dormant” game plan in a host of areas — from hiring, permitting, time and attendance to billing, 311 requests and customer service.</p><p>“It’s frustrating. … They make utilization of AI out to be a boogeyman and the reality is that there are ways you can incorporate it that will allow for the worker to be more efficient,” said Villegas, former chair of the City Council's Committee on Economic, Capital and Technology Development.</p><p>“We’re not talking about eliminating any jobs," Villegas continued. "We’re talking about allowing the worker to do more, because now they have some assistance through AI, which has been proven to make the product more effective and the process more efficient. At a time when we’re looking to cut costs, technology is the path that’s going to help create millions of dollars in savings.”</p><p>Glockner also wants his auditors to determine whether taxpayers are getting their money’s worth when it comes to the tens of millions of dollars being spent on community violence intervention.</p><p>“You’ve got a small number of groups that get large amounts of money that they then pass through other groups — which are doing … the legwork on the ground, and those groups have varying levels of sophistication and experience,” Glockner said. “It is absolutely appropriate for our office to be trying to ensure that this money which is going to solve or attempt to solve one of the city’s most critical problems is being well spent.”</p><p>Johnson has signed an executive order to begin the potentially costly process of delivering on his promise to create a stand-alone city department focusing exclusively on reducing and preventing gun violence.</p><p>But Finance Chair and 3rd Ward Ald. Pat Dowell wants to make certain that community violence intervention is working first.</p><p>Asked whether the inspector general's report would be done before the 2027 budget is passed, Glockner said, “It is an area where we are active, and I expect us to become more active. ... It would be great to have this by the time the budget needs to get hashed out, [but] that’s just not possible because of the scale of the work that needs to be done, the data to be viewed, the number of interviews to be done.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-310000" name="html-embed-module-310000"></a><iframe allow="monetization" frameborder="0" height="200" scrolling="no" src="https://play.prx.org/e?ge=prx_12963_db9c4288-21ec-4bf0-8517-83324d3b8aa5&uf=https%3A%2F%2Fpublicfeeds.net%2Ff%2F12963%2Ffeed-rss.xml " style="min-width: 300px;" width="100%"></iframe> </div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Bears report: RB D'Andre Swift returns to practice, Kyle Monangai still out
entries.summary: <p>What happened Thursday at Halas Hall:</p><h3>Swift back — Monangai not yet</h3><p>Running backs D'Andre Swift and Kyle Monangai both missed Wednesday's practice. Swift (hip/knee) returned Thursday, albeit on a limited basis,but Monangai did not.</p><p>Coach Ben Johnson was clear this week that Monangai (toe/thumb) was dealing more with the soreness of the Bears' 89-play offensive showing — he had 30 carries — than any one specific malady. It wouldn't be surprising to see him practice Friday.</p><p>Swift was benched after fumbling in the third quarter. He said he understood that fumbling "can't happen — and I'll take whatever comes with that" as punishment.</p><p>As for the rushing workload, offensive coordinator Press Taylor said "our ideal would be if both of those guys come out of the game with pretty even carries" because "they complement each other well."</p><h3>O-line intact </h3><h3></h3><p>After practicing without three-fifths of their offensive line Wednesday, the Bears had all five back. Right tackle Darnell Wright (ankle), right guard Jonah Jackson (ankle) and left guard Joe Thuney (pectoral muscle) were limited.</p><p>The Bears continued to practice without quarterback Caleb Williams (hamstring). Linebacker Keyshaun Elliott (quad), who was hurt Wednesday, sat out.</p><h3>KOR not OK</h3><h3></h3><p>After averaging just 17.5 yards on four Zavion Thomas kick returns Sunday, the Bears average a league-worst 21.3 yards per return. They committed three penalties on kick returns Sunday, though one was declined.</p><p>"We just gotta be better there, and it starts with me," special teams coordinator Richard Hightower said.</p>

entries.title: Reward boosted to $35K for info on slaying of OEMC dispatcher Natalia Rodriguez
entries.summary: <p>City and federal officials have increased a reward to $35,000 for information leading to the arrest of those responsible for the killing of an Office of Emergency Management and Communications dispatcher last month.</p><p>Natalia Rodriguez was fatally shot Sept. 11 in the Back of the Yards neighborhood. </p><p>Rodriguez, 50, was driving in the 4500 block of South Wood Street when she was struck by gunfire multiple times, causing her to crash into a parked SUV, Chicago police and the Cook County Crime Stoppers said. She was taken to Stroger Hospital where she died, police said.</p><p>Crime Stoppers initially offered a $10,000 reward, but now the federal Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives has added $20,000, and the Fraternal Order of Police Lodge 7, the union for rank-and-file Chicago cops, added another $5,000, according to a statement from Crime Stoppers. </p><p>A news conference is scheduled for 4:30 p.m. Friday in the 4500 block of South Wood Street to encourage anyone who may have witnessed the shooting or who has information about the person or persons responsible to come forward, according to Crime Stoppers.</p><p>In a statement issued shortly after the attack, Mary May, of the OEMC, expressed the office's “deepest condolences” to her family.</p><p>“Throughout her decade of service to this department, Natalia was a close colleague and friend to many who worked alongside her,” May said in the statement.</p><p>“Professionally, she was a hard worker and dedicated call-taker. Natalia’s passing is a terrible loss to her family and to OEMC. Her contributions to 911 Operations and the City of Chicago will not be forgotten,” the statement concluded.</p><p>Tipsters can remain completely anonymous, according to Crime Stoppers. No name is required, and individuals submitting information will receive a code number that can be used to claim an approved reward.</p><p>Submit a tip by calling the Cook County Crime Stoppers Tip Line: 800-535-7867 or online at: <a class="Link" href="http://www.cpdtip.com/" target="_blank" >www.CPDTIP.com</a></p>

entries.title: CATCH-22: Rivalry between Bears and 'Cheeseball Packs' runs deep
entries.summary: <p>Analyzing the Bears with the help of 22 names, starting with …</p><p></p><p><b>Malik Muhammad</b> <b>(1)</b>, who turned around at his locker, reached into his backpack and pulled out a black Moleskine notebook, the kind with a ribbon for a bookmark, on Wednesday.</p><p></p><p>The Bears cornerback, a fourth-round rookie, flipped through his notes and found the list he drafted at the start of the season.</p><p></p><p>At the top, in cursive: “Teams that passed on me — that rent is DUE!”</p><p></p><p>Below it is a list of teams that took cornerbacks ahead of the former Texas star, sorted by which week they play the Bears this season.</p><p></p><p>“I’m just checking them off the list,” he told me Wednesday.</p><p></p><p>The Jets, who drafted cornerback <b>D’Angelo Ponds</b> <b>(2)</b> in Round 2, were first. He put a check mark next to them after the Bears beat them Sunday.</p><p></p><p>Next? The Packers, who took <b>Brandon Cisse (3)</b> in the second round. Only Muhammad didn’t call them that on the list.</p><p></p><p>“Cheeseball Packs Boooooo,” he wrote.</p><p></p><p>With six o’s.</p><p></p><p>“Oh my God, wait ‘til we beat them,” he said.</p><p></p><p>The rivalry runs deep, even for the newest Bears. For others, it’s become part of their lives. Chairman<b> George McCaskey (4)</b> carries business cards that he hands out to Packers fans that says “it’s not too late to become a Bears fan.” Tight end <b>Cole Kmet</b> <b>(5)</b>, whose sister dates Packers defensive end <b>Lukas Van Ness (6)</b>, joked before the playoffs in January that he doesn't speak to her during rivalry week.</p><p></p><p>Receivers coach <b>Antwaan Randle El (7)</b>, who went to Thornton Township High School, can't walk into Lambeau Field without thinking of the rivalry games he grew up watching on TV. <b>Al Harris (8)</b>, the Bears' defensive backs coach, went to two Pro Bowls as a Packers cornerback from 2003-09 and is in the team’s hall of fame. The rivalry, he said, is different than any other in the NFL — it’s rooted in actual hate.</p><p></p><p>“I think just the core of it, it won’t stop,” he said. “It’s great.”</p><p></p><p>Linebacker <b>T.J. Edwards’</b> <b>(9)</b> wife is from Little Chute, Wis., about a half-hour southwest of Green Bay. His in-laws remain Packers fans. His father-in-law will wear an Edwards jersey to Lambeau Field on Sunday — but only with a Packers turtleneck underneath.</p><p></p><p>Edwards, who went to Lakes Community High School in Lake Villa and then Wisconsin, grew up a Bears fan. He can rattle off his favorite plays in the rivalry — linebacker <b>Lance Briggs’</b> <b>(10)</b> pick-six on Christmas Day 2005 and <b>Devin Hester’s</b> <b>(11)</b> 84-yard touchdown punt return touchdown in his NFL debut the following year. Both were at Lambeau Field.</p><p></p><p>He understands the rub with his in-laws.</p><p></p><p>“I think it explains the rivalry perfectly,” he said. “I literally married into the family and they still have a hard time fully converting. I respect it.”</p><p></p><h3>Ready for his rivalry debut is …</h3><p></p><p><b>Dayo Odeyingbo (12)</b>, the Bears defensive lineman who tore his Achilles’ tendon last year before the teams played three times in six weeks.</p><p></p><p>Odeyingbo’s family had made plans to come out for the regular-season home game against the Packers at Soldier Field, using his tickets. Players on injured reserve aren’t allowed to stand on the Bears’ sideline, though, so Odeyingbo dropped his family off at the Soldier Field players’ entrance and kept driving. <b>Chris Williams (13)</b>, who played defensive line for the Bears last year, had a 60<sup>th</sup>-floor apartment overlooking the stadium and told Odeyingbo he could watch the game from his couch.</p><p></p><p>Odeyingbo would look out the window, see celebrations after Bears touchdowns and then wait for the TV delay to catch up. That’s how he learned DJ Moore caught the 46-yard walk-off touchdown in overtime.</p><p></p><p>“For such a magical season, the way it played out at the end and into the playoffs,” he said, “it really hurt to not play in the games and really be at the games.”</p><p></p><p>Odeyingbo has been a big reason why the Bears defense has outperformed expectations, posting three sacks in four games. Last year he had just one over eight games before getting hurt.</p><p></p><h3>The last Bears QB to win more than one career game at Lambeau Field was …</h3><p></p><p><b>Rex Grossman</b> <b>(14)</b>, who won three-straight from 2004-06. Since then, four Bears quarterbacks have won once there: <b>Caleb Williams (15)</b>, <b>Jay Cutler (16)</b>, <b>Josh McCown</b> <b>(17)</b> and <b>Brian Griese (18)</b>. If <b>Tyson Bagent (19)</b> follows suit, he’d be the third Bears quarterback who wasn’t a Week 1 starter to win there in 20 years, compared to only two who were.</p><h3></h3><h3>Who hated being green?</h3><p></p><p><b>Kermit the Frog (20)</b>, or maybe Bears fans. There are three green teams in the NFL, and the Bears have played them three weeks in a row — the Eagles, Jets and Packers. The Packers will look different than at any other point in the 214 meetings of the rivalry, though, as they’ll debut their “Rivalries” uniform Sunday.</p><p></p><p>The set was unveiled in August, with Nike describing it as “a desaturated vintage green jersey with delicate alabaster and gold stripes, paired with alabaster pants and a matching matte helmet.” The alabaster is supposed to symbolize the paper of Packers stock certificates.</p><p></p><p>The Bears will wear their own alternate when they host the Packers on Christmas Day.</p><p></p><h3>Maybe they’re assembling an NBA team …</h3><h3></h3><p>Linebacker <b>Chris Paul</b> <b>(21)</b> and cornerback <b>Cobee Bryant</b> <b>(22)</b> tried out for the Packers this week.<br></p>

entries.title: Peoples Gas rate hike should be cut in half, ICC regulatory judges say
entries.summary: <p>Less than half of a $144 million rate hike requested by Peoples Gas is justifiable, according to a ruling this week by state administrative law judges that will affect how much Chicago residents pay on their heating bills this winter.</p><p>Instead, staffers for the Illinois Commerce Commission on Tuesday recommended that the panel should allow Chicago’s natural gas utility a collective increase next year totaling $66 million.</p><p>Peoples Gas <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/business/2026/01/05/peoples-gas-rate-hike-chicago-heating-bills" target="_blank" ><u>initially sought</u></a> a hike of $202 million to wrap up work on its beleaguered <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/consumer-affairs/2023/11/16/23963198/peoples-gas-rate-hike-pipeline-replacement-program-illinois-commerce-commission" target="_blank" ><u>pipeline replacement program</u></a> that regulators have ordered the company to scale back after years of running over budget and behind schedule.</p><p>Facing <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/05/06/illinois-attorney-general-kwame-raoul-rate-cut-request-peoples-gas-202m-hike-proposal" target="_blank" ><u>sweeping criticism</u></a> from consumer advocates, City Council members and Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul’s office, the utility — owned by Milwaukee-based WEC Energy Group, which reported a $1.6 billion profit last year — lowered its request over the summer.</p><p>Regulators on the commission are expected to issue a final ruling next month to conclude the quasi-judicial process that determines how much utilities are allowed to charge customers.</p><p>A $144 million rate hike would raise the average residential bill by as much as $8 starting in January. It wasn’t immediately clear what impact a $66 million hike would have.</p><p>Regulators granted Peoples Gas a hike of more than $300 million in 2023 when they clamped down on the pipeline replacement program.</p><p>“We are reviewing the administrative law judges’ recommendation,” a Peoples Gas spokesman said in an email. “As their proposed order states, our work to retire 1,000 miles of old pipe is “a binding safety mandate — not … a discretionary program whose costs can be reduced without serious consequences.</p><p>“We look forward to continuing to work with the Illinois Commerce Commission to meet its mandate of retiring old energy pipes nearing the end of their useful lives.”</p><p>Abe Scarr, director of the Illinois Public Interest Research Group, said the law judges’ proposed order “gets some important things right” on reining in the pipeline program, but “instead of acting on these findings, the order punts to a future investigation.”</p><p>“It's time to end the Peoples Gas pipe replacement program as we know it, and redirect the utility’s safety spending on the primary safety risks to its system,” Scarr said in a statement. “After more than a decade of failed pipe replacement spending, it's time for a new approach that properly prioritizes safety, doesn’t unnecessarily raise rates, and facilitates the transition to safer, cleaner energy.”</p><p>Consumer watchdogs at the Citizens Utility Board say “more fat can be trimmed.”</p><p>“This is a step in the right direction, but we urge the ICC to go even further than the proposed order, at a time when it has never been more crucial for regulators to combat unwarranted utility costs,” CUB General Counsel Eric DeBellis said in a statement. “In recent years, Commissioners have proven vigilant in cutting gas rate hikes beyond the levels recommended by proposed orders, and we hope they exercise that prudence again in this Peoples Gas case by lowering consumer costs further.”</p>

entries.title: Bridgeport vibra con aficionados de los White Sox que anhelan llegar a los playoffs desde hace 120 años
entries.summary: <p>Para la primera semana de octubre, los estacionamientos alrededor de Rate Field suelen volver a su condición de desierto de asfalto para su período de hibernación de seis meses.</p><p>Al menos ese fue el caso durante los últimos cuatro años, con los White Sox acumulando 405 derrotas desde su última participación en una postemporada en 2021.</p><p>Y así ha sido en todo el lado sur la mayoría de los otoños desde que el presidente Theodore Roosevelt estaba en el cargo y la ciudad todavía se reconstruía tras el Gran incendio de Chicago.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-760000" name="module-760000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Incluso en las 10 temporadas en la historia de la franquicia en que los fanáticos de los Sox pudieron disfrutar del béisbol de otoño en su estadio, no han vivido la euforia de sellar una serie de playoffs en casa desde el 14 de octubre de 1906.</p><p>En aquel entonces era difícil conseguir fotos, así que solo pueden imaginarse la escena en las gradas de madera del ya desaparecido parque, cerca de Pershing y Princeton, donde la actuación completa de Doc White selló un campeonato de la Serie Mundial sobre Orval Overall y esos fastidiosos Cubs.</p><p>Avancemos rápido 120 años, súmale la gracia de un fan en el Vaticano, espolvorea un relevista que agita una varita mágica y convoca la magia de un clubhouse joven y aguerrido —y los fanáticos de los Sox seguían entusiasmados afuera del parque el miércoles, acercándose a una fiesta de <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/10/06/white-sox-anticipating-raucous-crowd-seek-to-clinch-first-postseason-series-victory-at-home-since-1906-sean-burke-will-venable-chris-getz-tristan-peters-miguel-vargas-erick-fedde" target="_blank" >más de un siglo en gestación</a>.</p><p>Una desalentadora <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/10/07/white-sox-pitchers-issue-seven-walks-hitters-strike-out-14-times-in-alds-game-3-loss-to-guardians-jose-ramirez-miguel-vargas-colson-montgomery-munetaka-murakami" target="_blank" >derrota de 9-3</a> ante los Guardians en el Juego 3 de la Serie Divisional de la Liga Americana hizo que la fiel fanaticada de los Sox tuviera que esperar otro día para un posible triunfo decisivo. Pero no se van a ningún lado.</p><p>“Hemos estado esperando esto por tanto tiempo”, dijo Nikki Tieman mientras hacía tailgating con familiares y compañeros de trabajo en el lote C, tres horas antes </div> </div><p>“Estamos disfrutándolo muchísimo porque tuvimos un par de años difíciles. Seguíamos yendo a los juegos, seguíamos haciéndoles porras y usando nuestra ropa del equipo. Pero este año todo se siente un poco más dulce”, dijo Tieman. “Es un año mágico en el que todo parece alinearse por arte de magia, así que de seguro que el Papa está poniendo su pequeño granito de arena”.</p><p>Pero la familia de Tieman ha acompañado al equipo desde mucho antes de que Rob, de Dolton, se convirtiera en el Papa León XIV. La familia de Joliet tenía boletos de temporada en la línea de primera base en el viejo Comiskey Park, mucho después de que su tío Larry Vásquez tuviera su primer dolor de cabeza con los Sox al escucharlos por radio en 1959, cuando perdieron la Serie Mundial ante los Dodgers.</p><p>“No ganamos, pero ya sabes, a mí no me importó. Yo seguía apoyando”, dijo Vásquez, compartiendo una angustia discreta y multigeneracional demasiado familiar para los fanáticos de los Sox.</p><h3>Siguiendo a los Sox desde Irak</h3><p>El hermano de Tieman, Miguel Vásquez, estaba contento sólo de haber conseguido entradas. No pudo hacerlo en 2005, mientras servía en el Ejército de Estados Unidos en Irak, donde el internet lo dejó tan frustrado en su intento por comprar boletos para su familia como dejó a miles de aficionados de Chicago este año en la carrera por asientos de postemporada.</p><p>“Lo intenté muchísimo, pero el internet era pésimo allá”, dijo Vásquez, moviendo la cabeza por aquella transacción fallida 21 años después de esa temporada mágica de los Sox.</p><p>Pero sus compañeros de servicio sabían que no podían permitir que un camarada fanático de corazón se perdiera la magia.</p><p>“Me estaba poniendo el equipo, listo para salir, y se detuvieron, y me dijeron, ‘No. Tú vas a ir a ver el Juego 4 [que aseguró la Serie Mundial]’”, contó Miguel Vazquez, riéndose al recordar a su oficial aquella decisiva victoria de la Serie Mundial en Houston.</p><p>“Hoy estamos tratando de recuperar las buenas vibras de 2005”, dijo el menor de los Wisniewski, de Algonquin.</p><p>Esas buenas vibras brillaron por su ausencia en su tailgate de hace dos años, en el cumpleaños de Rich, durante la peor temporada de todos los tiempos de los Sox, con 121 derrotas en 2024. Fueron el único vehículo en el enorme lote, mientras legiones de fanáticos perdían la fe en una organización que estaba marcando el estándar moderno de la inutilidad en las Grandes Ligas.</p><p>“El béisbol es casa, así que para nosotros fue otro día en el parque, o sea, estuvo genial”, dijo John. “Pero era deprimente. Y era como: no podemos esperar hasta ganar y volver a ser grandes”.</p><p>“Me encanta ver esto”, dijo Rich, quien hizo de su hijo un fanático de los Sox.</p><p>“Uno no se convierte en fan de los Sox. Se nace fan de los Sox”, dijo John. “Es tu papá, es tu tío, es tu familia — todos los que son fanáticos de los Sox, y te traen aquí, y cada vez que vienes se siente como en casa”.</p><div entries.title: What happens when an elite runner competes in her first marathon? Emma Grace Hurley will find out Sunday
entries.summary: <p>One of the best runners on the U.S. road circuit over the last three years, Emma Grace Hurley is running her first <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-marathon" >marathon Sunday in Chicago</a>. Hurley decided 2026 was the perfect time for her to jump to a marathon, and she’s been training for 26.2 miles since June.</p><p>But <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports/2026/10/06/2026-chicago-marathon-what-to-know-how-to-watch" >as Sunday’s race approaches</a>, Hurley has some questions about the mental adjustment to the increased distance.</p><p>“There’s a bit of 'I don’t know what I don’t know yet.’ That will be interesting,” Hurley told the Chicago Sun-Times. “But as far as training goes, what I’ve learned to do is focus less on the result and focus more on the effort and what it should feel like, and with that the result will follow.”</p><p>Hurley, 28, has had strong results during her career, carrying into a successful 2026.</p><p>Based in Indianapolis, Hurley won Chicago’s 8K Shamrock Shuffle in March with an American-record time of 24 minutes and 29 seconds. Then in April, she won the USA Track & Field 10-mile national title championship in Washington, D.C. Just three weeks ago, she finished fifth in the World Half Marathon Championships in Copenhagen, completing the course in 66 minutes and 23 seconds.</p><p>Now she’s taking the next step — well, a lot of additional steps — in Chicago, one of eight elite marathons across the world.</p><p>Hurley, who said running marathons has been on her mind since graduating from Furman University in 2020, shifted from Atlanta to Indianapolis on Dec. 29, 2023, during what she called a “hectic time” to choose to move. Over that time, she’s grown more comfortable in road races, especially the half-marathon, and got increasingly excited about going 26.2 miles.</p><p>Hurley will make her debut at that distance in front of her parents, extended family and her boyfriend. She’ll do that at an event known for fast times because of the relatively flat course and how the race’s setup is planned with the runners in mind.</p><p>“I know it’s kind of funny because Chicago is a place you go to run fast, but for me I’m more focused on the effort and where I finish within the field than the time. For me, that’s brought a lot of comfort,” Hurley said. “As far as tackling the distance, I don’t know, but I think the goal is to try to be relaxed and just enjoy the first half and then over the second half is where I think I’ll really have to dig deep.”</p><p>The second half, of course, is the terrain Hurley hasn’t experienced. She does have a plan to help her break through a wall, if one comes up during her run.</p><p>In short, she won’t forget the effort she put in before the race. Not just in training with coach Andrew Begley during a warm summer, but the way she’s lived her life for the last four-plus months.</p><p>“At that point, it’s an hour left. It’s just reminding myself that I can do something hard for an hour, two hours because I spent months and months with every decision I’ve made has been about setting myself up for [the marathon],” Hurley said. “And I don’t just mean every running decision, I mean every [other] decision. Do I go to this thing my friends are doing or not? What time do I go to bed? How far do I walk? I mean every decision has been about setting up this day correctly.</p><p>“It’s almost like I’ve gotten to that 26-mile mark and there’s point-two to go, and it’s just paying attention for that amount of time,” she added. “I can do that.”</p>

entries.title: White Sox would open American League Championship Series at 7 p.m. Monday
entries.summary: <p>If the White Sox hold off the Guardians' comeback bid, they'll play Game 1 of the American League Championship Series at 7 p.m. Monday in St. Petersburg, Florida, against the Rays. </p><p>MLB released the broadcast schedule Thursday for the best-of-seven ALCS, which will air on TBS, truTV and HBO Max. Game 2 is set for 7 p.m. Tuesday in St. Pete, followed by Games 3-5 at Rate Field. Games 3 and 4 are scheduled for 4 p.m., though Game 4 would move to 7 p.m. if the National League Championship Series between the Brewers and Dodgers ends in four games.</p><p>If necessary, Game 5 is set for 7 p.m., Game 6 for 4 p.m. and Game 7 for 7 p.m. If the NLCS doesn't go the distance, ALCS Game 6 would move to 7 p.m.</p>
